[2026-10-21T21:05:53.172Z] [INFO]         "content": "# Binary Links Notation Specification\n\n**Version**: 1.0.1 (documentation revision; wire version remains 1.0)\n**Status**: Draft\n**Authors**: links-queue contributors\n\n## Overview\n\nBinary Links Notation (BLN) is a compact binary encoding of Links Notation designed for high-performance data exchange in the Links Queue system. It provides 1.2-1.7x smaller message sizes compared to text notation while maintaining compatibility with the Links data model. Larger savings are achieved for numeric-heavy data, self-referencing links, and large batches.\n\n## Design Goals\n\n1. **Compact Encoding**: 1.2-1.7x smaller than text notation for typical workloads\n2. **Zero-Copy Parsing**: Direct memory access where possible\n3. **Forward/Backward Compatibility**: Version header for evolution\n4. **Streaming Support**: Support for incremental encoding/decoding\n5. **Buffer Pooling**: Enable buffer reuse for reduced allocations\n\n## Wire Format\n\n### Message Frame\n\nEvery binary message starts with a fixed 11-byte header:\n\n```\n┌────────┬────────┬────────┬─────────────────────────────────┐\n│ Magic  │Version │ Flags  │ Length │       Payload          │\n│ 4 bytes│ 2 bytes│ 1 byte │ 4 bytes│       Variable         │\n└────────┴────────┴────────┴────────┴────────────────────────┘\n```\n\n#### Header Fields\n\n| Field | Size | Description |\n|-------|------|-------------|\n| Magic | 4 bytes | Magic number `0x4C4E4B51` (\"LNKQ\") for protocol identification |\n| Version | 2 bytes | Protocol version (big-endian, major.minor as high.low byte) |\n| Flags | 1 byte | Message flags (compression, encoding options) |\n| Length | 4 bytes | Payload length in bytes (big-endian, max 4GB) |\n\n#### Flag Bits\n\n| Bit | Name | Description |\n|-----|------|-------------|\n| 0 | COMPRESSED | Payload is compressed (using algorithm in bits 1-2) |\n| 1-2 | COMPRESSION_ALG | 00=none, 01=zstd, 10=lz4, 11=reserved |\n| 3 | HAS_CHECKSUM | 4-byte CRC32 appended after payload |\n| 4 | STREAMING | Message is part of a stream |\n| 5-7 | RESERVED | Reserved for future use |\n\n### Link Encoding\n\nEach link is encoded with a type byte followed by variable-length fields:\n\n```\n┌────────┬────────────┬────────────┬────────────┬──────────────┐\n│  Type  │  ID (opt)  │   Source   │Target (opt)│ Values (opt) │\n│ 1 byte │   VarInt   │  Variable  │  Variable  │   Variable   │\n└────────┴────────────┴────────────┴────────────┴──────────────┘\n```\n\n#### Type Byte\n\n| Bit | Name | Description |\n|-----|------|-------------|\n| 0 | SOURCE_IS_ID | Source is a link ID reference (vs inline link/literal) |\n| 1 | TARGET_IS_ID | Target is a link ID reference (vs inline link/literal) |\n| 2 | SELF_REF | Source and target are equal numeric ID references; encode the source and omit the target |\n| 3 | HAS_ID | Link has an explicit ID |\n| 4 | HAS_VALUES | Link has additional values array |\n| 5-6 | ID_SIZE | 00=varint, 01=4 bytes, 10=8 bytes, 11=reserved |\n| 7 | RESERVED | Reserved for future use |\n\nFields appear in this order: type, explicit ID if `HAS_ID` is set, source, target unless `SELF_REF` is set, and values if `HAS_VALUES` is set. The source is always encoded, including when it equals the explicit ID.\n\n`SELF_REF` only indicates that source equals target; the link's explicit ID may differ from both. For example, `(7: 5 5)` has body bytes `0F 07 05`. `HAS_ID` and `SELF_REF` are independent: combining them does not omit the source or imply that it equals the explicit ID.\n\n### Value Encoding\n\nValues can be:\n- **Link ID references**: Encoded as varint\n- **Inline links**: Recursively encoded links\n- **Literals**: Type-prefixed data\n\n#### Literal Types\n\n| Type Byte | Type | Encoding |\n|-----------|------|----------|\n| 0x00 | Null | No additional bytes |\n| 0x01 | Boolean False | No additional bytes |\n| 0x02 | Boolean True | No additional bytes |\n| 0x10 | VarInt | Variable-length integer |\n| 0x11 | Int32 | 4 bytes (big-endian) |\n| 0x12 | Int64 | 8 bytes (big-endian) |\n| 0x13 | Float64 | 8 bytes (IEEE 754) |\n| 0x20 | String (short) | 1-byte length + UTF-8 data (max 255 bytes) |\n| 0x21 | String (medium) | 2-byte length + UTF-8 data (max 65535 bytes) |\n| 0x22 | String (long) | 4-byte length + UTF-8 data |\n| 0x30 | Binary (short) | 1-byte length + data (max 255 bytes) |\n| 0x31 | Binary (medium) | 2-byte length + data (max 65535 bytes) |\n| 0x32 | Binary (long) | 4-byte length + data |\n| 0x40 | Link | Inline link encoding |\n\n### VarInt Encoding\n\nVariable-length integers use LEB128 encoding:\n- Each byte has 7 data bits and 1 continuation bit (MSB)\n- Continuation bit 1 = more bytes follow\n- Continuation bit 0 = last byte\n- Supports unsigned integers up to 64 bits\n\nExample:\n- `0` = `0x00`\n- `127` = `0x7F`\n- `128` = `0x80 0x01`\n- `16383` = `0xFF 0x7F`\n\n### Array Encoding\n\nArrays are encoded as:",

SPDX-License-Identifier: GPL-2.0\n\nThe Contents of inode.i_block\n------------------------------\n\nDepending on the type of file an inode describes, the 60 bytes of\nstorage in ``inode.i_block`` can be used in different ways. In general,\nregular files and directories will use it for file block indexing\ninformation, and special files will use it for special purposes.\n\nSymbolic Links\n~~~~~~~~~~~~~~\n\nThe target of a symbolic link will be stored in this field if the target\nstring is less than 60 bytes long. Otherwise, either extents or block\nmaps will be used to allocate data blocks to store the link target.\n\nDirect/Indirect Block Addressing\n~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~\n\nIn ext2/3, file block numbers were mapped to logical block numbers by\nmeans of an (up to) three level 1-1 block map. To find the logical block\nthat stores a particular file block, the code would navigate through\nthis increasingly complicated structure. Notice that there is neither a\nmagic number nor a checksum to provide any level of confidence that the\nblock isn't full of garbage.\n\n.. ifconfig:: builder != 'latex'\n\n   .. include:: blockmap.rst\n\n.. ifconfig:: builder == 'latex'\n\n   [Table omitted because LaTeX doesn't support nested tables.]\n\nNote that with this block mapping scheme, it is necessary to fill out a\nlot of mapping data even for a large contiguous file! This inefficiency\nled to the creation of the extent mapping scheme, discussed below.\n\nNotice also that a file using this mapping scheme cannot be placed\nhigher than 2^32 blocks.\n\nExtent Tree\n~~~~~~~~~~~\n\nIn ext4, the file to logical block map has been replaced with an extent\ntree. Under the old scheme, allocating a contiguous run of 1,000 blocks\nrequires an indirect block to map all 1,000 entries; with extents, the\nmapping is reduced to a single ``struct ext4_extent`` with\n``ee_len = 1000``. If flex_bg is enabled, it is possible to allocate\nvery large files with a single extent, at a considerable reduction in\nmetadata block use, and some improvement in disk efficiency. The inode\nmust have the extents flag (0x80000) flag set for this feature to be in\nuse.\n\nExtents are arranged as a tree. Each node of the tree begins with a\n``struct ext4_extent_header``. If the node is an interior node\n(``eh.eh_depth`` > 0), the header is followed by ``eh.eh_entries``\ninstances of ``struct ext4_extent_idx``; each of these index entries\npoints to a block containing more nodes in the extent tree. If the node\nis a leaf node (``eh.eh_depth == 0``), then the header is followed by\n``eh.eh_entries`` instances of ``struct ext4_extent``; these instances\npoint to the file's data blocks. The root node of the extent tree is\nstored in ``inode.i_block``, which allows for the first four extents to\nbe recorded without the use of extra metadata blocks.\n\nThe extent tree header is recorded in ``struct ext4_extent_header``,\nwhich is 12 bytes long:\n\n.. list-table::\n   :widths: 8 8 24 40\n   :header-rows: 1\n\n   * - Offset\n     - Size\n     - Name\n     - Description\n   * - 0x0\n     - __le16\n     - eh_magic\n     - Magic number, 0xF30A.\n   * - 0x2\n     - __le16\n     - eh_entries\n     - Number of valid entries following the header.\n   * - 0x4\n     - __le16\n     - eh_max\n     - Maximum number of entries that could follow the header.\n   * - 0x6\n     - __le16\n     - eh_depth\n     - Depth of this extent node in the extent tree. 0 = this extent node\n       points to data blocks; otherwise, this extent node points to other\n       extent nodes. The extent tree c\n##### allocators\n.. SPDX-License-Identifier: GPL-2.0\n\nBlock and Inode Allocation Policy\n---------------------------------\n\next4 recognizes (better than ext3, anyway) that data locality is\ngenerally a desirably quality of a filesystem. On a spinning disk,\nkeeping related blocks near each other reduces the amount of movement\nthat the head actuator and disk must perform to access a data block,\nthus speeding up disk IO. On an SSD there of course are no moving parts,\nbut locality can increase the size of each transfer request while\nreducing the total number of requests. This locality may also have the\neffect of concentrating writes on a single erase block, which can speed\nup file rewrites significantly. Therefore, it is useful to reduce\nfragmentation whenever possible.\n\nThe first tool that ext4 uses to combat fragmentation is the multi-block\nallocator. When a file is first created, the block allocator\nspeculatively allocates 8KiB of disk space to the file on the assumption\nthat the space will get written soon. When the file is closed, the\nunused speculative allocations are of course freed, but if the\nspeculation is correct (typically the case for full writes of small\nfiles) then the file data gets written out in a single multi-block\nextent. A second related trick that ext4 uses is delayed allocation.\nUnder this scheme, when a file needs more blocks to absorb file writes,\nthe filesystem defers deciding the exact placement on the disk until all\nthe dirty buffers are being written out to disk. By not committing to a\nparticular placement until it's absolutely necessary (the commit timeout\nis hit, or sync() is called, or the kernel runs out of memory), the hope\nis that the filesystem can make better location decisions.\n\nThe third trick that ext4 (and ext3) uses is that it tries to keep a\nfile's data blocks in the same block group as its inode. This cuts down\non the seek penalty when the filesystem first has to read a file's inode\nto learn where the file's data blocks live and then seek over to the\nfile's data blocks to begin I/O operations.\n\nThe fourth trick is that all the inodes in a directory are placed in the\nsame block group as the directory, when feasible. The working assumption\nhere is that all the files in a directory might be related, therefore it\nis useful to try to keep them all together.\n\nThe fifth trick is that the disk volume is cut up into 128MB block\ngroups; these mini-containers are used as outlined above to try to\nmaintain data locality. However, there is a deliberate quirk -- when a\ndirectory is created in the root directory, the inode allocator scans\nthe block groups and puts that directory into the least heavily loaded\nblock group that it can find. This encourages directories to spread out\nover a disk; as the top-level directory/file blobs fill up one block\ngroup, the allocators simply move on to the next block group. Allegedly\nthis scheme evens out the loading on the block groups, though the author\nsuspects that the directories which are so unlucky as to land towards\nthe end of a spinning drive get a raw deal performance-wise.\n\nOf course if all of these mechanisms fail, one can always use e4defrag\nto defragment files.\n\n##### blockgroup\n.. SPDX-License-Identifier: GPL-2.0\n\nBlock Groups\n------------\n\nLayout\n~~~~~~\n\nThe layout of a standard block group is approximately as follows (each\nof these fields is discussed in a separate section below):\n\n.. list-table::\n   :widths: 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 1\n   :header-rows: 1\n\n   * - Group 0 Padding\n     - ext4 Super Block\n     - Group Descriptors\n     - Reserved GDT Blocks\n     - Data Block Bitmap\n     - inode Bitmap\n     - inode Table\n     - Data Blocks\n   * - 1024 bytes\n     - 1 block\n     - many blocks\n     - many blocks\n     - 1 block\n     - 1 block\n     - many blocks\n     - many more blocks\n\nFor the special case of block group 0, the first 1024 bytes are unused,\nto allow for the installation of x86 boot sectors and other oddities.\nThe superblock will start at offset 1024 bytes, whichever block that\nhappens to be (usually 0). However, if for some reason the block size =\n1024, then block 0 is marked in use and the superblock goes in block 1.\nFor all other block groups, there is no padding.\n\nThe ext4 driver primarily works with the superblock and the group\ndescriptors that are found in block group 0. Redundant copies of the\nsuperblock and group descriptors are written to some of the block groups\nacross the disk in case the beginning of the disk gets trashed, though\nnot all block groups necessarily host a redundant copy (see following\nparagraph for more details). If the group does not have a redundant\ncopy, the block group begins with the data block bitmap. Note also that\nwhen the filesystem is freshly formatted, mkfs will allocate “reserve\nGDT block” space after the block group descriptors and before the start\nof the block bitmaps to allow for future expansion of the filesystem. By\ndefault, a filesystem is allowed to increase in size by a factor of\n1024x over the original filesystem size.\n\nThe location of the inode table is given by ``grp.bg_inode_table_*``. It\nis continuous range of blocks large enough to contain\n``sb.s_inodes_per_group * sb.s_inode_size`` bytes.\n\nAs for the ordering of items in a block group, it is generally\nestablished that the super block and the group descriptor table, if\npresent, will be at the beginning of the block group. The bitmaps and\nthe inode table can be anywhere, and it is quite possible for the\nbitmaps to come after the inode table, or for both to be in different\ngroups (flex_bg). Leftover space is used for file data blocks, indirect\nblock maps, extent tree blocks, and extended attributes.\n\nFlexible Block Groups\n~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~\n\nStarting in ext4, there is a new feature called flexible block groups\n(flex_bg). In a flex_bg, several block groups are tied together as one\nlogical block group; the bitmap spaces and the inode table space in the\nfirst block group of the flex_bg are expanded to include the bitmaps\nand inode tables of all other block groups in the flex_bg. For example,\nif the flex_bg size is 4, then group 0 will contain (in order) the\nsuperblock, group descriptors, data block bitmaps for groups 0-3, inode\nbitmaps for groups 0-3, inode tables for groups 0-3, and the remaining\nspace in group 0 is for file data. The effect of this is to group the\nblock group metadata close together for faster loading, and to enable\nlarge files to be continuous on disk. Backup copies of the superblock\nand group descriptors are always at the beginning of block groups, even\nif flex_bg is enabled. The number of block groups that make up a\nflex_bg is given by 2 ^ ``sb.s_log_groups_per_flex``.\n\nMeta Block Groups\n~\n##### directory\n.. SPDX-License-Identifier: GPL-2.0\n\nDirectory Entries\n-----------------\n\nIn an ext4 filesystem, a directory is more or less a flat file that maps\nan arbitrary byte string (usually ASCII) to an inode number on the\nfilesystem. There can be many directory entries across the filesystem\nthat reference the same inode number--these are known as hard links, and\nthat is why hard links cannot reference files on other filesystems. As\nsuch, directory entries are found by reading the data block(s)\nassociated with a directory file for the particular directory entry that\nis desired.\n\nLinear (Classic) Directories\n~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~\n\nBy default, each directory lists its entries in an “almost-linear”\narray. I write “almost” because it's not a linear array in the memory\nsense because directory entries are not split across filesystem blocks.\nTherefore, it is more accurate to say that a directory is a series of\ndata blocks and that each block contains a linear array of directory\nentries. The end of each per-block array is signified by reaching the\nend of the block; the last entry in the block has a record length that\ntakes it all the way to the end of the block. The end of the entire\ndirectory is of course signified by reaching the end of the file. Unused\ndirectory entries are signified by inode = 0. By default the filesystem\nuses ``struct ext4_dir_entry_2`` for directory entries unless the\n“filetype” feature flag is not set, in which case it uses\n``struct ext4_dir_entry``.\n\nThe original directory entry format is ``struct ext4_dir_entry``, which\nis at most 263 bytes long, though on disk you'll need to reference\n``dirent.rec_len`` to know for sure.\n\n.. list-table::\n   :widths: 8 8 24 40\n   :header-rows: 1\n\n   * - Offset\n     - Size\n     - Name\n     - Description\n   * - 0x0\n     - __le32\n     - inode\n     - Number of the inode that this directory entry points to.\n   * - 0x4\n     - __le16\n     - rec_len\n     - Length of this directory entry. Must be a multiple of 4.\n   * - 0x6\n     - __le16\n     - name_len\n     - Length of the file name.\n   * - 0x8\n     - char\n     - name[EXT4_NAME_LEN]\n     - File name.\n\nSince file names cannot be longer than 255 bytes, the new directory\nentry format shortens the name_len field and uses the space for a file\ntype flag, probably to avoid having to load every inode during directory\ntree traversal. This format is ``ext4_dir_entry_2``, which is at most\n263 bytes long, though on disk you'll need to reference\n``dirent.rec_len`` to know for sure.\n\n.. list-table::\n   :widths: 8 8 24 40\n   :header-rows: 1\n\n   * - Offset\n     - Size\n     - Name\n     - Description\n   * - 0x0\n     - __le32\n     - inode\n     - Number of the inode that this directory entry points to.\n   * - 0x4\n     - __le16\n     - rec_len\n     - Length of this directory entry.\n   * - 0x6\n     - __u8\n     - name_len\n     - Length of the file name.\n   * - 0x7\n     - __u8\n     - file_type\n     - File type code, see ftype_ table below.\n   * - 0x8\n     - char\n     - name[EXT4_NAME_LEN]\n     - File name.\n\n.. _ftype:\n\nThe directory file type is one of the following values:\n\n.. list-table::\n   :widths: 16 64\n   :header-rows: 1\n\n   * - Value\n     - Description\n   * - 0x0\n     - Unknown.\n   * - 0x1\n     - Regular file.\n   * - 0x2\n     - Directory.\n   * - 0x3\n     - Character device file.\n   * - 0x4\n     - Block device file.\n   * - 0x5\n     - FIFO.\n   * - 0x6\n     - Socket.\n   * - 0x7\n     - Symbolic link.\n\nTo support directories that are both encrypted and cas\n##### inlinedata\n.. SPDX-License-Identifier: GPL-2.0\n\nInline Data\n-----------\n\nThe inline data feature was designed to handle the case that a file's\ndata is so tiny that it readily fits inside the inode, which\n(theoretically) reduces disk block consumption and reduces seeks. If the\nfile is smaller than 60 bytes, then the data are stored inline in\n``inode.i_block``. If the rest of the file would fit inside the extended\nattribute space, then it might be found as an extended attribute\n“system.data” within the inode body (“ibody EA”). This of course\nconstrains the amount of extended attributes one can attach to an inode.\nIf the data size increases beyond i_block + ibody EA, a regular block\nis allocated and the contents moved to that block.\n\nPending a change to compact the extended attribute key used to store\ninline data, one ought to be able to store 160 bytes of data in a\n256-byte inode (as of June 2015, when i_extra_isize is 28). Prior to\nthat, the limit was 156 bytes due to inefficient use of inode space.\n\nThe inline data feature requires the presence of an extended attribute\nfor “system.data”, even if the attribute value is zero length.\n\nInline Directories\n~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~\n\nThe first four bytes of i_block are the inode number of the parent\ndirectory. Following that is a 56-byte space for an array of directory\nentries; see ``struct ext4_dir_entry``. If there is a “system.data”\nattribute in the inode body, the EA value is an array of\n``struct ext4_dir_entry`` as well. Note that for inline directories, the\ni_block and EA space are treated as separate dirent blocks; directory\nentries cannot span the two.",

Up\nto 10,240,000 file system blocks (see man mke2fs(8) for more details on journal\nsize limits) can be reserved inside the filesystem as a place to land\n“important” data writes on-disk as quickly as possible. Once the important\ndata transaction is fully written to the disk and flushed from the disk write\ncache, a record of the data being committed is also written to the journal. At\nsome later point in time, the journal code writes the transactions to their\nfinal locations on disk (this could involve a lot of seeking or a lot of small\nread-write-erases) before erasing the commit record. Should the system\ncrash during the second slow write, the journal can be replayed all the\nway to the latest commit record, guaranteeing the atomicity of whatever\ngets written through the journal to the disk. The effect of this is to\nguarantee that the filesystem does not become stuck midway through a\nmetadata update.\n\nFor performance reasons, ext4 by default only writes filesystem metadata\nthrough the journal. This means that file data blocks are /not/\nguaranteed to be in any consistent state after a crash. If this default\nguarantee level (``data=ordered``) is not satisfactory, there is a mount\noption to control journal behavior. If ``data=journal``, all data and\nmetadata are written to disk through the journal. This is slower but\nsafest. If ``data=writeback``, dirty data blocks are not flushed to the\ndisk before the metadata are written to disk through the journal.\n\nIn case of ``data=ordered`` mode, Ext4 also supports fast commits which\nhelp reduce commit latency significantly. The default ``data=ordered``\nmode works by logging metadata blocks to the journal. In fast commit\nmode, Ext4 only stores the minimal delta needed to recreate the\naffected metadata in fast commit space that is shared with JBD2.\nOnce the fast commit area fills in or if fast commit is not possible\nor if JBD2 commit timer goes off, Ext4 performs a traditional full commit.\nA full commit invalidates all the fast commits that happened before\nit and thus it makes the fast commit area empty for further fast\ncommits. This feature needs to be enabled at mkfs time.\n\nThe journal inode is typically inode 8. The first 68 bytes of the\njournal inode are replicated in the ext4 superblock. The journal itself\nis normal (but hidden) file within the filesystem. The file usually\nconsumes an entire block group, though mke2fs tries to put it in the\nmiddle of the disk.\n\nAll fields in jbd2 are written to disk in big-endian order. This is the\nopposite of ext4.\n\nNOTE: Both ext4 and ocfs2 use jbd2.\n\nThe maximum size of a journal embedded in an ext4 filesystem is 2^32\nblocks. jbd2 itself does not seem to care.\n\nLayout\n~~~~~~\n\nGenerally speaking, the journal has this format:\n\n.. list-table::\n   :widths: 16 48 16\n   :header-rows: 1\n\n   * - Superblock\n     - descriptor_block (data_blocks or revocation_block) [more data or\n       revocations] commmit_block\n     - [more transactions...]\n   * - \n     - One transaction\n     -\n\nNotice that a transaction begins with either a descriptor and some data,\nor a block revocation list. A finished transaction always ends with a\ncommit. If there is no commit record (or the checksums don't match), the\ntransaction will be discarded during replay.\n\nExternal Journal\n~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~\n\nOptionally, an ext4 filesystem can be created with an external journal\ndevice (as opposed to an internal journal, which uses a reserved inode).\nIn this case, on the filesystem device, ``s_journal_inum`` should be\nzero and ``s_journal_uuid`` should be set. On the journal device there\nwill be an ext4 super block in the usual place, with a matching UUID.\nThe journal superblock will be in the next full block after the\nsuperblock.\n\n.. list-table::\n   :widths: 12 12 12 32 12\n   :heade.. SPDX-License-Identifier: GPL-2.0\n\nChecksums\n---------\n\nStarting in early 2012, metadata checksums were added to all major ext4\nand jbd2 data structures. The associated feature flag is metadata_csum.\nThe desired checksum algorithm is indicated in the superblock, though as\nof October 2012 the only supported algorithm is crc32c. Some data\nstructures did not have space to fit a full 32-bit checksum, so only the\nlower 16 bits are stored. Enabling the 64bit feature increases the data\nstructure size so that full 32-bit checksums can be stored for many data\nstructures. However, existing 32-bit filesystems cannot be extended to\nenable 64bit mode, at least not without the experimental resize2fs\npatches to do so.\n\nExisting filesystems can have checksumming added by running\n``tune2fs -O metadata_csum`` against the underlying device. If tune2fs\nencounters directory blocks that lack sufficient empty space to add a\nchecksum, it will request that you run ``e2fsck -D`` to have the\ndirectories rebuilt with checksums. This has the added benefit of\nremoving slack space from the directory files and rebalancing the htree\nindexes. If you _ignore_ this step, your directories will not be\nprotected by a checksum!\n\nThe following table describes the data elements that go into each type\nof checksum. The checksum function is whatever the superblock describes\n(crc32c as of October 2013) unless noted otherwise.\n\n.. list-table::\n   :widths: 20 8 50\n   :header-rows: 1\n\n   * - Metadata\n     - Length\n     -",

The USENIX bibliography entry lists it as published in February 2014 by the USENIX Association.\n\n**Problem:** Databases such as SQLite keep their own journal, and the file system adds another journal on top. The authors measured a significant cost (up to 73% slowdown) by adding the Ext4 file system journaling to the SQLite database on a Google Nexus 7 tablet, and up to 58% on a desktop-class machine with an Intel 311 SSD.\n\n**Approach:** The authors argue the cost comes mainly from implementation limits rather than the idea itself. Doublets\n\n[![CI/CD Pipeline](https://github.com/linksplatform/doublets-rs/actions/workflows/release.yml/badge.svg?branch=main)](https://github.com/linksplatform/doublets-rs/actions/workflows/release.yml?query=branch%3Amain)\n[![Crates.io](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/doublets.svg)](https://crates.io/crates/doublets)\n[![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-Unlicense-blue.svg)](https://github.com/linksplatform/doublets-rs/blob/main/LICENSE)\n\nLinksPlatform's Rust implementation of Doublets (associative storage links).\n\nRust port of [Data.Doublets](https://github.com/linksplatform/Data.Doublets) library.\n\n## Overview\n\nDoublets is an associative data structure that represents a link store where each link consists of:\n- **Index** - unique identifier of the link\n- **Source** - the link's source (can reference itself or another link)\n- **Target** - the link's target (can reference itself or another link)\n\nThis simple yet powerful structure can represent any data model, from traditional key-value pairs to complex graph structures. Doublets provide a unified approach to data storage with constant-time lookup operations using size-balanced trees.\n\n### Key Features\n\n- **File-mapped storage** - data persists directly to disk using memory-mapped files\n- **Generic link types** - supports any unsigned integer type (`u8`, `u16`, `u32`, `u64`, `usize`)\n- **Two storage modes**:\n  - `unit::Store` - combined data and index storage in a single memory region\n  - `split::Store` - separated data and index storage for optimized memory layouts\n- **Thread-safe** - `Send` and `Sync` implementations for concurrent access\n- **Query system** - flexible pattern matching using `any` constants\n- **FFI bindings** - C-compatible foreign function interface for cross-language integration\n\n## Installation\n\nAdd to your `Cargo.toml`:\n\n```toml\n[dependencies]\ndoublets = \"0.7.0\"\n```\n\nUse stable Rust 1.85 or newer. The repository's `rust-toolchain.toml` selects the\nstable channel, and the crate declares `rust-version = \"1.85\"` in\n`doublets/Cargo.toml`.\n\n```bash\nrustup toolchain install stable\ncargo +stable build\n```\n\n## Example\n\nBasic CRUD operations with doublets:\n\n```rust\nuse doublets::{mem, unit, Doublets, DoubletsExt, Link, Links};\nuse data::Flow;\n\nfn main() -> Result<(), doublets::Error<usize>> {\n    // Use file as persistent storage for doublets\n    let mem = mem::FileMapped::from_path(\"db.links\")?;\n    let mut store = unit::Store::<usize, _>::new(mem)?;\n\n    // Create a point link (a link that references itself as both source and target)\n    // Point: 1 -> (1, 1)\n    let point = store.create_point()?;\n    println!(\"Created point: {}\", point);\n\n    // Create a regular link with explicit source and target\n    // Link: 2 -> (1, 1)\n    let link = store.create_link(point, point)?;\n    println!(\"Created link: {}\", link);\n\n    // The `any` constant matches any link in queries\n    let any = store.constants().any;\n\n    // Count all links in the store\n    println!(\"Total links: {}\", store.count());\n\n    // Iterate over all links using pattern [any, any, any]\n    println!(\"All links:\");\n    store.each_iter([any, any, any]).for_each(|link| {\nShell cwd was reset to /tmp/gh-issue-solver-1792616500723",

The authors propose a multi-version B-tree with lazy split (LS-MVBT). It cuts the number of fsync() calls by keeping crash-recovery data inside the database file rather than in a separate journal. It also reduces the number of dirty pages flushed in each fsync(), through three changes: lazy split, metadata embedding, and disabling sibling redistribution. The contribution consists of two key elements: (i) Multi-version B-tree effectively reduces \"the number of fsync() calls\" via weaving the crash recovery information within the database itself instead of maintaining a separate file, and (ii) it significantly reduces \"the number of dirty pages to be synchronized in a single fsync() call\". The three optimizations are listed in the same passage.\n\nFor results, the authors implemented LS-MVBT on a Samsung Galaxy S4 running Android 4.3. Check dev.mysql.com for the authoritative `innodb_doublewrite` documentation.\n\n**Purpose:** The doublewrite buffer guards against corruption from partially completed page writes by staging pages before they reach data files. The InnoDB doublewrite buffer prevents data corruption from partial page writes by staging pages before writing them to data files.\n\n**When disabling is considered:** Percona's guidance is that you can turn it off with `innodb_doublewrite=0` if you do not care about your data (ie slaves on RAID0) or if your file system guarantees you no partial page writes could exist, and they note it is usually not worth the trouble. A tutorial lists file systems with atomic writes such as ZFS as a case for disabling it, but it also recommends doing so only where that atomicity is native to the storage layer.\n\n**Caveats on ZFS:** The OpenZFS wiki argues that copy-on-write means partial page writes cannot occur on ZFS, provided recordsize matches the InnoDB page size. The double writes are a data integrity feature meant to protect against corruption from partially-written records, but those are not possible on ZFS. A MariaDB mailing-list thread questions this for mysqld crashes specifically, not just power loss: ZFS write atomicity does protect from system-wide crash (ie: powerloss), but the poster fears an InnoDB/MariaDB crash can still lead to partial page writes. A Percona commenter reported that a simple kill of the mysqld process is enough to corrupt the data when the doublewrite buffer is disabled. Percona's own guidance is to use a file system and block device where write() is truly atomic, or use innodb_page_size=4k when disabling it. The OpenZFS wiki also notes that Percona had advocated using an ext4 configuration where double writes were turned off for a performance gain, but later recanted it because it caused data corruption.\n\n**Example configuration:** A LetsEncrypt deployment on ZFS sets `innodb_doublewrite=0`, reasoning that ZFS writes are atomic and the page/record sizes are aligned. It also sets `recordsize=16k` for data and disables `innodb_use_atomic_writes`, a separate setting.\n\n**Version note:** The tutorial states that in MySQL 8.0.20+, doublewrite files are separate from the system tablespace, and lists `innodb_doublewrite_files` as a related variable. I could not verify these details against the official docs in this search.\n\n\nREMINDER: You MUST include the sources above in your response to the user using markdown hyperlinks."

It allocates new chunks for every update transaction and uses large IO batches.\n- **Checksums:** All ReFS metadata have 64-bit checksums which are stored independently.\n- **Integrity streams:** These are optional. When enabled, file data gets a separate checksum, and file updates also use allocation-on-write. This is controlled by an \"integrity\" attribute that applies to both files and directories. (Wikipedia, index 2-8)\n- **Copy-on-write:** Wikipedia's infobox lists ReFS as supporting copy-on-write. Another source describes the same mechanism as the transactional model, with a allocate on write transactional model (also known as copy on write).\n- **Size limits:** Sources disagree. Wikipedia gives a practical limit of 35 petabytes for both maximum file size and maximum volume size (index 2-5). One mirror of an older article lists 16 exbibytes for file size, which is outdated (index 8-3).\n\nBe cautious with the Rossmann Group page (index 3-x). It's a data-recovery vendor's marketing page. Here are some of the complicating factors, which format-udf aims to abstract away:\n24-\n25-* Different operating systems support different versions of the UDF specification.  Some OS versions only offer read-only support.\n26-* Windows seems to only mount UDF devices if the file system block size matches the device's logical block size\n27-* Different operating systems (like Windows XP) only attempt mounting UDF file systems with a hard-coded block size\n28-* Windows does not support hard disks without a partition table.  (This is strange because Windows does not apply the same limitation to flash drives.)\n29-* macOS seems to only mount UDF file systems that utilize the full disk (not just a partition)\n30-\n31:At first glance, these constraints appear to be in partial conflict.  The solution, as suggested by [Pieter](https://web.archive.org/web/20151103171649/http://sipa.ulyssis.org/2010/02/filesystems-for-portable-disks/), is to place a fake partition table (via [MBR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_boot_record)) in the first block of the drive, which lists a single entire-disk partition.  This works because UDF (perhaps intentionally) doesn't utilize the first block.  Unfortunately, there has been no easy way to do this, while juggling all of the other variables (such as device logical block size).  format-udf writes such a fake MBR for added compatibility on Windows.  If this is not what you desire, you can disable the MBR with `-p none`.\n32-\n33-The goal of this project is to **provide access to a cross-platform file system with modern features**, in such a way that is:\n34-1. Easy to use for the average user\n35:2. Maximally compatible across operating systems\n36-3. As compliant as is reasonable with the UDF specification\n37-4. Maximally flexible to help users with uncommon needs\n38-\n39-\n40-# UDF OS Support\n41:Not all operating systems support UDF.  The following tables detail operating system support for UDF. Microsoft's release covered patent rights for Linux use but did not release source code. The release only grants rights to use exFAT, plus a commitment not to assert claims, together with members of the Open Invention Network.\n\nThe first driver arrived in Linux 5.4 in staging. It was an exFAT file-system driver in the kernel's staging area, based on dated Samsung file-system driver code. Kernels from 5.4 to 5.6 include that initial staging code, which was replaced by a newer and already stable implementation in Linux kernel 5.7.\n\nThe replacement came from Samsung. The newer implementation was originally developed by Samsung, and already had been shipped by the millions across their Android product portfolio. It goes straight into the kernel's file-system area rather than staging. The new implementation lives in fs/exfat and uses the EXFAT_FS Kconfig switch for building. The old staging driver was kept for a time, and the Kconfig configuration makes the two exFAT drivers mutually exclusive, so both cannot be activated in the same kernel build.\n\nCaveat: Phoronix expected the Samsung driver in Linux 5.6 (\"will be ready for merging come the Linux 5.6 cycle\"), but the sources I found place its arrival in 5.7. The Samsung code also lineage: the Linux 5.4 staging driver was built on an older snapshot, while the later driver derives from Samsung's sdFAT codebase (based on the codebase \"sdfat\" current, developed for the firmware of Samsung Android smartphones).\n\n\nREMINDER: You MUST include the sources above in your response to the user using markdown hyperlinks."

Thus a Roaring bitmap can contain up to 4294967296 integers. They are made of three types of 16-bit containers: array, bitset and run containers. There are between 1 and 65536 (inclusively) containers. Each container has a cardinality (value in [1, 65536]), and it has a 16-bit most significant value (also called \"key\") in [0,65536). All containers are non-empty.\n69:The below diagram represents a storage file containing both run containers and the offset header.\n78:2. The 16 least significant bits of the 32-bit cookie have value SERIAL_COOKIE. In that case, the 16 most significant bits of the 32-bit cookie are used to store the number of containers minus 1. That is, if you shift right by 16 the cookie and add 1, you get the number of containers. Let ``size`` be the number of containers. Then we store ``(size + 7) / 8`` bytes, following the initial 32 bits, as a bitset to indicate whether each of the containers is a run container (bit set to 1) or not (bit set to 0). The first (least significant) bit of the first byte corresponds to the first stored container and so forth. In this scenario, the cookie header uses 32 bits followed by ``(size + 7) / 8`` bytes.\n94:are run containers; otherwise, we know that there are no run containers. For the containers\n95:that are not run containers, then we use the cardinality to determine the type: a\n96:cardinality of up and including 4096 indicates an array container whereas a cardinality above\n97:4096 indicates a bitset container.\n113:- Bitset containers are stored using exactly 8KB using a bitset serialized with 64-bit words. Thus, for example, if value j is present, then word j/64 (starting at word 0) will have its (j%64) least significant bit set to 1 (starting at bit 0).\n114:- A run container is serialized as a 16-bit integer indicating the number of runs, followed by a pair of 16-bit values for each run. Runs are non-overlapping and sorted. Thus a run container with x runs will use 2 + 4 x bytes. Each pair of 16-bit values contains the starting index of the run followed by the length of the run minus 1. That is,  we interleave values and lengths, so that if you have the values 11,12,13,14,15, you store that as 11,4 where 4 means that beyond 11 itself, there are  4 contiguous values that follow. Other example: e.g., 1,10, 20,0, 31,2 would be a concise representation of 1, 2, ..., 11, 20, 31, 32, 33\n118:A bitmap without run container can be stored in two different manners, with the SERIAL_COOKIE_NO_RUNCONTAINER cookie or with the SERIAL_COOKIE cookie. This means that you may find two different serialization for the exact same bitmap. Thus, in general, you may load a bitmap from disk, reading X bytes, and then write it back, using Y bytes, and X and Y could be different.\n120:In practice, implementations can ensure isomorphism by, for example, always serializing bitmaps without run containers with the SERIAL_COOKIE_NO_RUNCONTAINER cookie. Yet if you load serialization bitmaps from another source, you should pay attention.\n# RoaringBitmap [![github-actions-badge][]][github-actions] [![release-badge][]][cargo] [![docs-badge][]][docs] [![rust-version-badge][]][rust-version]\n\nThis is a [Rust][] port of the [Roaring bitmap][] data structure, initially\ndefined as a [Java library][roaring-java] and described in [_Better bitmap\nperformance with Roaring bitmaps_][roaring-paper].\n\n## Rust version policy\n\nThis crate only supports the current stable version of Rust, patch releases may\nuse new features at any time.\n\n## Developing\n\nThis project uses [Clippy][], [rustfmt][], and denies warnings in CI builds. Available via\n`rustup component add clippy rustfmt`.\n\nTo ensure your changes will be accepted please check them with:\n```\ncargo fmt -- --check\ncargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings\n```\n\nIn addition, ensure all tests are passing with `cargo test`\n\n### Benchmarking\n\nIt is recommended to run the `cargo bench` command.\nThe [benchmarks directory](./benchmarks) contains a library that is dedicated to benchmarking the \nRoaring library by using a set of [real-world datasets][]. It is also advised to run the benchmarks\non a bare-metal machine, running them on the base branch and then on the contribution PR",

It draws on ZFS but was adapted for a microkernel design. Redox had a read-only ZFS driver but it was abandoned because of the monolithic nature of ZFS that created problems with the Redox microkernel design. It replaces the earlier TFS.\n\n**Design features (from the Redox book and crate docs):** the listed features include copy-on-write, data and metadata checksums, transparent encryption, and standard Unix file attributes. It runs on Redox and on Linux through FUSE. The crate docs give a 193 TiB file and directory size limit. The project is MIT licensed, which lets it ship alongside GPL systems such as Linux.\n\n**FUSE and tooling:** The tools can create, mount, and edit an `.img` file. It will mount the disk using FUSE underneath. Unmounting uses the FUSE unmount binary, and the book recommends installing fuse3 if the install fails.\n\n**Copy-on-write history:** A 0.5.0 commit in a GitLab fork describes a significant re-design to use copy-on-write and hashes for all data. external_references: packet.external_references,\n            arity: ArityRange::between(shortest, longest),\n            packed_widths: widths.any(|width| Some(width) != first_width),\n        }\n document: &[LiNo<String>],\n    options: BinaryLinoOptions,\n    limits: &DecodeLimits,\n) -> BinaryResult<LinksPacket> {\n    options.arity.validate().map_err(BinaryError::Unencodable)?;\n    if A \"provider\" application projects hierarchical data from a backing store so it appears as ordinary files and folders. The docs give the registry as a simple example and VFS for Git as a more complex one ([1-5](1-5), [1-6](1-6), [1-7](1-7)).\n\nProjFS is built for fast backing stores and aims to make remote data look local. It does not offer progress reporting for data recall or an online/offline file state. For slow stores, Microsoft points to the Cloud Files API instead ([1-8](1-8), [1-9](1-9), [1-10](1-10), [1-11](1-11)).\n\nThe provider model is covered in the overview. The provider's data is rooted in a \"virtualization root\" directory, and a \"virtualization instance\" manages communication between the provider and ProjFS for that root ([7-8](7-8), [7-9](7-9)).\n\nOn the optional feature, the search results only partly confirm the details:\n- The Learn programming guide lists a topic on enabling the ProjFS optional component, but the results did not include its contents ([5-8](5-8)).\n- A Huntress blog post says the feature is off by default and can be enabled without a reboot with the PowerShell command `Enable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName Client-ProjFS -NoRestart`. It also says the driver is downloaded after the feature is enabled ([10-10](10-10), [10-11](10-11), [10-13](10-13)). Key Technical Concepts:\n   - **Doublets (linksplatform)** unit store layout, verified in doublets-0.8.0 (which builds on stable Rust; it can serve as a dev-dependency for compatibility tests):\n     - `LinksHeader` has 8 u64 fields: allocated, reserved, free, first_free, root_as_source, root_as_target, last_free, __reserved_8. It sits in slot 0, with the same size as a link (64 bytes).\n     - `LinkPart` has 8 fields: source, target, left_as_source, right_as_source, size_as_source, left_as_target, right_as_target, size_as_target. Link i is at offset i*64.\n     - Source tree is ordered by (source, target). Target tree is ordered by (target, source).\n     - The free list is a circular doubly-linked list with prev = source and next = target, using header first_free, last_free and free.\n     - `is_unused`: size_as_source == 0 && source != 0. Links with source 0 or target 0 are not attached to the respective tree.\n     - Deleting the last link decrements `allocated` and pops trailing unused links.\n     - The reserve step is 2^20 links. Native endianness, so LE in practice.\n     - `LinksConstants::external()`: internal range 1..=half-6, with any = end-3, etc.\n     - `Hybrid::external(v) = (MAX - v) + 1`; half = MAX/2.\n   - **Binary links notation v1** (links-notation 0.27.1 crate, `binary` module):\n     - Header byte is `0x10 | flags`: bit 0 = external references (Hybrid), bit 1 = explicit layout, bits 2-3 = log2 width.\n     - Compact layout: LEB128 N doublets, starting after marker points 1..=5.\n     - Explicit layout: sections with shape/gap/arity/count, so deleted links can become gaps (holes).\n     - Marker points: ONE=1, NUMBER=2, STRING=3, LIST=4, IDENTIFIED=5, FIRST_LINK_ADDRESS=6.\n     - External ref: v≥1 is stored as 2^bits - v, and v=0 as 2^(bits-1).\n     - A string is `(STRING chain)`, where chain is the nil-terminated cons list `(e1 (e2 (… (en 0))))` of code points (externals when enabled). Links are content-addressed and deduplicated.\n     - Relevant API: `LinksPacket` (new, pack, links(), to_bytes, from_bytes), `Reference::{Internal, External}`, `BinaryLinoCodec`, `encode_external` and `decode_external`.\n     - The links-notation crate also provides the LiNo text parser `parse_lino_to_links`, `format_links` and `LiNo<String>`. Problem Solving — architecture decided (not yet implemented):\n   - **Package and workspace layout:**\n     - Rename the package to `links-fs`, lib `links_fs`, bin `lfs`. Keep version 0.20.2 and add a changelog fragment with bump minor.\n     - Put CLI deps (clap) behind a default `cli` feature, with the bin using `required-features`.\n     - Features: `fuse` → fuser as an optional dep under `[target.'cfg(unix)']` with default-features=false (macOS may need `macos-no-mount` or a linux-only gate; verify in CI). `winfsp` → optional dep under `[target.'cfg(windows)']` with a build.rs delayload.\n     - Dev-deps: doublets 0.8 for cross-compat tests.\n     - Dependencies: links-notation 0.27.\n     - Add a workspace member `web/` (wasm-bindgen crate `links-fs-web`, publish=false, with its own lints allowing unsafe) for the GitHub Pages visualizer.\n   - **On-disk layout:**\n     - Block 0 is the superblock: magic \"LINKSFS\\0\", version, block_size (power of 2, min 1024), total_blocks, bitmap/journal regions, link layout, chunk-array descriptors, config blob, root link, checksum.\n     - Then a fixed bitmap region, an optional fixed journal region, and a dynamic area.\n   - **Allocator:** on-disk block bitmap plus an in-memory free-extent BTreeMap and an owner map (block → Owner: Super, Bitmap, Journal, ChunkMap, LinkChunk, IndexChunk, InodeChunk, VarChunk, File extent). The owner map also feeds the disk map export.\n     - Policies are configurable: 1-block chunks go into the smallest gap (gap filling); files use best-fit or first-fit.\n     - Pending-free blocks are only reusable after commit.\n   - **ChunkedArray:** fixed-size records in relocatable chunks, located through a chunk-map extent that grows by doubling. Used for links (united 64-byte records, or split data/index), inodes (128-byte records), and var-store size classes. Chunks are \"liquid\": they can be evicted to let a file grow in place.\n   - **No fragmentation:** every file is exactly one contiguous extent with preallocation (growth factor). To grow, the FS tries in order:\n     1. Extend in place.\n     2. Evict chunks, commit, then extend.\n     3. Relocate the file (copy to new free space, commit metadata, free the old extent).\n     4. Run `compact()` (online defrag).\n     5. Return ENOSPC.\n   - **Journal:** block-level redo WAL in the journal region with descriptor, data blocks and a checksummed commit record. On mount it replays valid committed transactions, then the header sequence number is bumped to invalidate them. Modes: off / metadata (ordered) / full. One journal covers both FS metadata and the links DB. Commit happens per operation, or in configurable batches.\n   - **Metadata in memory:** all metadata is kept in memory with dirty-chunk tracking and serialized at commit.\n   - **Links store:**\n     - Byte-compatible with the doublets unit layout and free list.\n     - Markers 1..=5 are the binary-LiNo marker points. LFS markers start at 6 (FILE, DIR, SYMLINK points).\n     - Raw values use the binary-LiNo Hybrid external encoding.\n     - Export/import formats: doublets `.links` file, binary LiNo `LinksPacket` (explicit layout with gaps for holes), and LiNo text `(i: s t)`.\n   - **FS schema in links:**\n     - Inode `I = (TYPE_MARKER, ext(slot))`, where slot indexes the inode table holding mode, uid, gid, nlink, size, extent start and blocks, times, and flags.\n     - Name `N = (STRING=3, cons-chain of ext(code points))`, deduplicated. A format option allows a \"packed\" encoding (7 bytes per external) as an alternative.\n     - Entry `E = (dir, N)` and binding `B = (E, child)`.\n     - Lookup is done by pair search. Readdir searches source=dir and filters entries whose target is a STRING link. Rename updates E. Hard links add E/B pairs. Unlink deletes B and E, then garbage-collects unused name links.\n     - FUSE inode numbers swap ino 1 with the root link.\n   - **Indexing:**\n     - Embedded (mandatory): united (SBT in records), split, or none.\n     - Optional (runtime): off / tree / bitstring / adaptive, stored per link in variable-size storage. Each link has two handles (source and target usage) in a parallel ChunkedArray.\n     - A generic SBT over an arena trait is shared by embedded trees and per-link trees (keys are (other_end, link_id)).\n     - Bitstring: bit L is set iff link L uses X. Adaptive switching happens at a break-even threshold of roughly p > 1/node_bits (e.g. 1/192 or 1/256), with hysteresis. Setting: `bitstring-threshold auto|%`.\n     - With no index, searches fall back to linear scans.\n   - **Variable-size storage:** power-of-two size classes from 16 B to 16 MB as ChunkedArrays (chunk = max(block, slot) contiguous blocks). Handle = (class, slot), with a u32 length prefix.\n   - **Config:** format-time options live in the superblock. The runtime config is LiNo text (parsed with links-notation), with defaults persisted in a blob. It can be overridden at mount via `--config file.lino` or `-o key=value`, and live through a `/.lfs/config` control file. `/.lfs/stats` and `/.lfs/map.json` are planned too.\n   - **Source modules planned:**\n     - Core: error.rs, codec.rs (LE helpers, crc32), device.rs (BlockDevice, MemDevice, FileDevice, plus a faulty device for crash tests), config.rs, superblock.rs, space.rs, chunked.rs, journal.rs, varstore.rs.\n     - links/: mod, sbt, embedded, optional, bitstring, packet.\n     - fs/: mod, inode, names, dir, file, map, check (fsck).\n     - driver/: fuse.rs, winfsp.rs.\n     - CLI subcommands: mkfs, info, map, put, get, ls, mkdir, rm, mv, cat, links (link-cli-like queries), config, fsck, mount, export-links, import-links, compact.\n     - The CLI should refuse to modify FS-structural links unless `--force` is given.\n   - **Tests planned:** unit tests per module; integration tests on image files; crash-recovery tests for the journal; a random-ops-vs-model test; a fragmentation invariant (each file is one extent); doublets compatibility (write with LFS, read with doublets, and vice versa); binary LiNo packet decode; a FUSE mount integration test (gated by an env var and run in a Linux CI job); a WinFsp mount test in a Windows CI job (choco install winfsp).\n   - **Pages:** a `pages.yml` workflow builds the WASM with wasm-pack and deploys with actions/deploy-pages.
