[2026-10-22T00:38:43.756Z] [INFO]       {
[2026-10-22T00:38:43.756Z] [INFO]         "tool_use_id": "toolu_01HtD82qdqcTVJmM8CN8yPn7",
[2026-10-22T00:38:43.756Z] [INFO]         "type": "tool_result",
[2026-10-22T00:38:43.756Z] [INFO]         "content": "### 2.2 Measured cost of \"journaling of journal\" (JOJ)\n\n- **Jeong, Lee, Lee, Son, Won, \"I/O Stack Optimization for Smartphones\", USENIX ATC'13 (Best Paper)** ([page](https://www.usenix.org/conference/atc13/technical-sessions/presentation/jeong), [PDF](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/conference/atc13/atc13-jeong.pdf)):\n  - Named the **JOJ anomaly**: ext4 journals SQLite's own journal writes, and each SQLite `fsync()` triggers bulky ext4 journal commits.\n  - Fixes: no unnecessary metadata journaling, an external journal, and polling I/O. SQLite inserts/sec went up 130%. F2FS + WAL went from 39 to 157 inserts/sec (+300%).\n- **Kim, Nam, Park, Won, \"Resolving Journaling of Journal Anomaly in Android I/O: Multi-Version B-tree with Lazy Split\", FAST'14** ([page](https://www.usenix.org/conference/fast14/technical-sessions/presentation/kim-wook-hee)):\n  - Recovery information is woven *into the DB B-tree itself*, so no separate journal file is needed.\n  - Result: 704 inserts/s vs 416 for WAL (+70%) and 55 for TRUNCATE.\n- **Shen, Park, Zhu, \"Journaling of Journal Is (Almost) Free\", FAST'14** ([page](https://www.usenix.org/conference/fast14/technical-sessions/presentation/shen), [PDF](https://www.cs.rochester.edu/u/kshen/papers/fast2014.pdf)):\n  - Adding ext4 journaling under SQLite cost up to **73 %** on a Nexus 7 and **58 %** on an SSD desktop.\n  - The authors argue the cost comes from the implementation. With one I/O on the synchronous commit path and an *adaptive per-file journaling mode*, it drops to < 6 % (7 % faster on average).\n- **Lee et al., \"WALDIO: Eliminating the Filesystem Journaling in Resolving the Journaling of Journal Anomaly\", USENIX ATC'15** ([page](https://www.usenix.org/conference/atc15/technical-session/presentation/lee_wongun)):\n  - SQLite WAL writes go through direct I/O with preallocation, header embedding and group sync, skipping FS journaling.\n  - Result: 5.1× WAL insert throughput and 1/6 of the I/O volume.\n- **SQLite batch atomic write on F2FS** ([SQLite check-in](https://sqlite.org/src/info/532bbf1f2b1028db), [source](https://www.sqlite.org/src/info/2e0357c2ed309279)):\n  - With `SQLITE_ENABLE_BATCH_ATOMIC_WRITE`, SQLite collects a transaction in memory and commits it with `F2FS_IOC_START_ATOMIC_WRITE`/`COMMIT_ATOMIC_WRITE`, with no rollback journal at all.\n  - This is the \"FS offers transactions to the DB\" approach LFS can generalise.\n\n**Takeaway:** the cost is real (tens of percent up to several times) and can be removed in two ways. Either the DB stores its recovery data inside its own structure, or the FS exposes atomic/transactional writes the DB can use. LFS can do both, because the FS and the links database share one journal or COW commit.\n\n### 4.2 Space break-even derivation\n\nDefinitions:\n\n- `N` = size of the link address space (number of link slots).\n- `k` = number of links that use link `X` in a given role (for example, as source).\n- `ρ = k / N` = usage density of `X`.\n- `w` = address width in bits (64, or 32 for compact stores).\n- `p` = index words paid per member.\n\nCost of each representation for the set {links whose source is X}:\n\n| Representation | Bits | Notes |\n|---|---|---|\n| Embedded binary tree (SBT/AVL) | `p·w·k` with `p = 3` (left, right, size), so **192·k** for w = 64 | plus one root word |\n| Sorted array / B-tree leaf of addresses | ≈ `w·k` = **64·k** (B-tree adds about 1/fanout overhead) | |\n| Plain bitstring over the address space | **`N`** (or `max−min+1` if the range is tracked, as `BitString` does) | 1 bit per link: \"uses X as source?\" |\n\nThe bitstring is smaller when `N < p·w·k`, which gives\n\n> **ρ\\* = k/N = 1 / (p·w)**\n>\n> - Embedded tree, 64-bit: **ρ\\* = 1/192 ≈ 0.52 %**\n> - Embedded tree, 32-bit: 1/96 ≈ 1.04 %\n> - Sorted array, 64-bit: 1/64 ≈ 1.56 %\n> - Within a 2^16 chunk with 16-bit offsets (Roaring): 1/16, i.e. **4096 entries**\n\nSo a link referenced by more than about 0.5 % of all links is cheaper to index with a bitstring than with an embedded 64-bit tree.\n\n**Same rule in Roaring.** Roaring splits 32-bit space into 2^16-value chunks. A chunk is an **array container** (sorted `u16`, 16 bits per entry) up to and including **4096** entries, and a **bitmap container** (exactly 8 KiB = 65536 bits) above that. 65536 / 16 = 4096, which is the same formula with `p·w = 16`. Run containers (2 + 4·runs bytes) cover long consecutive ranges ([RoaringFormatSpec](https://github.com/RoaringBitmap/RoaringFormatSpec), [Lemire et al., *Better bitmap performance with Roaring bitmaps*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1402.6407), [*Consistently faster and smaller compressed bitmaps with Roaring*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.06549)).\n\n**Same rule, with hysteresis, in btrfs.** The free-space tree converts extents to bitmaps when `extent_count > bitmap_high_thresh = total_bitmap_bytes / sizeof(item)`, and back when below `high − 100` ([free-space-tree.c](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/master/fs/btrfs/free-space-tree.c)).\n\n**Caveats specific to links:**\n\n1. **Embedded tree slots are already paid for in unified mode.** The 6 index words exist in every link record whether used or not. A bitstring therefore only *saves* space if the layout is variable: a heavily-used X is moved to a bitstring index and its referrers' per-role tree slots are dropped or reused. This is the issue's \"variable size storage for optional indexing\". Otherwise the bitstring is extra cost, justified by speed.\n2. **N grows.** A fixed threshold `k > N/192` drifts as the store grows. Use **chunked bitstrings** (Roaring-like): split the address space into chunks of `C = 2^m` slots and choose per chunk between an offset array (`m` bits per entry), which wins below `C/m` entries, and a bitmap (`C` bits). The decision then depends only on local density, not on `N`.\n3. **Hysteresis.** Switch to a bitstring at `ρ > 1/(p·w)` and back only at, say, `ρ < 1/(2·p·w)`, to avoid flapping. btrfs uses an absolute margin of 100 items.\n\n### 4.3 Time break-even (why bitstrings may pay off earlier)\n\n| Operation | Tree (k members) | Bitstring (N bits) |\n|---|---|---|\n| membership test `X→Y?` | O(log k) dependent random reads | O(1): one word |\n| count | O(1) using the `Size` field | O(N/64) popcount unless cached |\n| enumerate all members | O(k) pointer chases (cache/disk misses) | O(N/64) sequential words + `tzcnt` |\n| insert/delete | O(log k) plus rebalancing writes (several records dirtied, which also costs journal volume) | O(1): one word dirtied |\n\nIf one random miss costs about `M` sequential word scans (M ≈ 50–200 for DRAM, far more for disk), enumeration is faster with a bitstring once `k·M > N/64`, i.e. **ρ > 1/(64·M)**. That is roughly 1/3200 to 1/12800, which is *much lower* than the space break-even. Fewer dirtied records per update also means a smaller journal. These are estimates and LFS should benchmark them. Make `p`, `w`, the chunk size and both thresholds runtime-configurable, as the issue requests.\n## Implications for LFS\n\n1. **Architecture: one OS-agnostic core, thin adapters.**\n   - The `lfs-core` crate holds the on-disk format, allocator, journal, links store and indexes. It runs on any `Read+Write+Seek` device (file image, raw device, in-memory, WASM).\n   - Adapters, in priority order:\n     - (a) **Linux/macOS: `fuser`** (MIT). Pure-rust mount on Linux needs no system libs to build. macOS needs macFUSE or FUSE-T at build time unless built with `macos-no-mount`.\n     - (b) **All three OSes: `nfsserve`** (BSD-3) localhost NFSv3. No kernel driver and pure Rust; the best path for macOS without a kext and for CI. Windows needs Pro or higher.\n     - (c) **Windows: WinFsp** for the best NTFS-like semantics. Because winfsp-rs is GPL-3.0, prefer **hand-written Unlicense FFI bindings to `winfsp-x64.dll`**, which WinFsp's FLOSS exception allows since the Unlicense is OSI-approved, or use **`dokan`** (MIT crate, LGPL DLL, no bindgen).\n     - (d) Later: **FSKit** Swift extension wrapping the Rust core (macOS 15.4+), and in-kernel drivers.\n   - RedoxFS (MIT, COW, fuser-based) is the closest existing template.\n2. **CI**:\n   - Core unit and property tests on ubuntu, macos and windows runners.\n   - FUSE mount tests on ubuntu (`modprobe fuse`, `apt install fuse3`; remove the non-setuid `/usr/local/bin/fusermount3`).\n   - WinFsp mount tests on windows (`choco install winfsp` plus a registry check; clang is preinstalled for bindgen if winfsp-sys is used).\n   - On macOS: build-only for FUSE, and NFS (`mount_nfs`) mount tests through `nfsserve`.\n3. **Anti-fragmentation techniques worth copying (simplified):**\n   - **extents** with a large or configurable max length (ext4 is capped at 128 MiB by a 15-bit length field; LFS can use 32- or 64-bit lengths);\n   - **delayed allocation** (allocate at flush, when the size is known);\n   - **per-file preallocation windows** plus **shared small-object arenas** (ext4 `mb_stream_req` = 16 blocks, `mb_group_prealloc` = 512);\n   - **free-space index by size class** (mballoc's largest-free-order and average-fragment-size lists, or a buddy allocator);\n   - **inline data** for tiny files;\n   - **flex_bg-like grouping** of metadata;\n   - **metadata checksums** (crc32c).\n   - ext4 still ages (FAST'17), so the strict \"no fragmentation\" goal needs either **online compaction/relocation** (like `EXT4_IOC_MOVE_EXT`) or the issue's idea: **fill gaps with small doublet links** so free space stays in a few large runs and small objects pack densely.\n4. **Single journal or commit for FS and database.** The JOJ literature (ATC'13, FAST'14 ×2, ATC'15) shows a 58–73 % to 5× penalty from stacked journals. SQLite inserts/sec went up 130%. F2FS + WAL went from 39 to 157 inserts/sec (+300%).\n- **Kim, Nam, Park, Won, \"Resolving Journaling of Journal Anomaly in Android I/O: Multi-Version B-tree with Lazy Split\", FAST'14** ([page](https://www.usenix.org/conference/fast14/technical-sessions/presentation/kim-wook-hee)):\n  - Recovery information is woven *into the DB B-tree itself*, so no separate journal file is needed.\n  - Result: 704 inserts/s vs 416 for WAL (+70%) and 55 for TRUNCATE.\n- **Shen, Park, Zhu, \"Journaling of Journal Is (Almost) Free\", FAST'14** ([page](https://www.usenix.org/conference/fast14/technical-sessions/presentation/shen), [PDF](https://www.cs.rochester.edu/u/kshen/papers/fast2014.pdf)):\n  - Adding ext4 journaling under SQLite cost up to **73 %** on a Nexus 7 and **58 %** on an SSD desktop.\n  - The authors argue the cost comes from the implementation. With one I/O on the synchronous commit path and an *adaptive per-file journaling mode*, it drops to < 6 % (7 % faster on average).\n- **Lee et al., \"WALDIO: Eliminating the Filesystem Journaling in Resolving the Journaling of Journal Anomaly\", USENIX ATC'15** ([page](https://www.usenix.org/conference/atc15/technical-session/presentation/lee_wongun)):\n  - SQLite WAL writes go through direct I/O with preallocation, header embedding and group sync, skipping FS journaling.\n  - Result: 5.1× WAL insert throughput and 1/6 of the I/O volume.\n- **SQLite batch atomic write on F2FS** ([SQLite check-in](https://sqlite.org/src/info/532bbf1f2b1028db), [source](https://www.sqlite.org/src/info/2e0357c2ed309279)):\n  - With `SQLITE_ENABLE_BATCH_ATOMIC_WRITE`, SQLite collects a transaction in memory and commits it with `F2FS_IOC_START_ATOMIC_WRITE`/`COMMIT_ATOMIC_WRITE`, with no rollback journal at all.\n  - This is the \"FS offers transactions to the DB\" approach LFS can generalise.\n\n**Takeaway:** the cost is real (tens of percent up to several times) and can be removed in two ways. Either the DB stores its recovery data inside its own structure, or the FS exposes atomic/transactional writes the DB can use. LFS can do both, because the FS and the links database share one journal or COW commit.\n\n### 4.2 Space break-even derivation\n\nDefinitions:\n\n- `N` = size of the link address space (number of link slots).\n- `k` = number of links that use link `X` in a given role (for example, as source).\n- `ρ = k / N` = usage density of `X`.\n- `w` = address width in bits (64, or 32 for compact stores).\n- `p` = index words paid per member.\n\nCost of each representation for the set {links whose source is X}:\n\n| Representation | Bits | Notes |\n|---|---|---|\n| Embedded binary tree (SBT/AVL) | `p·w·k` with `p = 3` (left, right, size), so **192·k** for w = 64 | plus one root word |\n| Sorted array / B-tree leaf of addresses | ≈ `w·k` = **64·k** (B-tree adds about 1/fanout overhead) | |\n| Plain bitstring over the address space | **`N`** (or `max−min+1` if the range is tracked, as `BitString` does) | 1 bit per link: \"uses X as source?\" |\n\nThe bitstring is smaller when `N < p·w·k`, which gives\n\n> **ρ\\* = k/N = 1 / (p·w)**\n>\n> - Embedded tree, 64-bit: **ρ\\* = 1/192 ≈ 0.52 %**\n> - Embedded tree, 32-bit: 1/96 ≈ 1.04 %\n> - Sorted array, 64-bit: 1/64 ≈ 1.56 %\n> - Within a 2^16 chunk with 16-bit offsets (Roaring): 1/16, i.e. **4096 entries**\n\nSo a link referenced by more than about 0.5 % of all links is cheaper to index with a bitstring than with an embedded 64-bit tree.\n\n**Same rule in Roaring.** Roaring splits 32-bit space into 2^16-value chunks. A chunk is an **array container** (sorted `u16`, 16 bits per entry) up to and including **4096** entries, and a **bitmap container** (exactly 8 KiB = 65536 bits) above that. 65536 / 16 = 4096, which is the same formula with `p·w = 16`. Run containers (2 + 4·runs bytes) cover long consecutive ranges ([RoaringFormatSpec](https://github.com/RoaringBitmap/RoaringFormatSpec), [Lemire et al., *Better bitmap performance with Roaring bitmaps*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1402.6407), [*Consistently faster and smaller compressed bitmaps with Roaring*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.06549)).\n\n**Same rule, with hysteresis, in btrfs.** The free-space tree converts extents to bitmaps when `extent_count > bitmap_high_thresh = total_bitmap_bytes / sizeof(item)`, and back when below `high − 100` ([free-space-tree.c](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/master/fs/btrfs/free-space-tree.c)).\n\n**Caveats specific to links:**\n\n1. **Embedded tree slots are already paid for in unified mode.** The 6 index words exist in every link record whether used or not. A bitstring therefore only *saves* space if the layout is variable: a heavily-used X is moved to a bitstring index and its referrers' per-role tree slots are dropped or reused. This is the issue's \"variable size storage for optional indexing\". Otherwise the bitstring is extra cost, justified by speed.\n2. **N grows.** A fixed threshold `k > N/192` drifts as the store grows. Use **chunked bitstrings** (Roaring-like): split the address space into chunks of `C = 2^m` slots and choose per chunk between an offset array (`m` bits per entry), which wins below `C/m` entries, and a bitmap (`C` bits). The decision then depends only on local density, not on `N`.\n3. **Hysteresis.** Switch to a bitstring at `ρ > 1/(p·w)` and back only at, say, `ρ < 1/(2·p·w)`, to avoid flapping. btrfs uses an absolute margin of 100 items.\n\n### 4.3 Time break-even (why bitstrings may pay off earlier)\n\n| Operation | Tree (k members) | Bitstring (N bits) |\n|---|---|---|\n| membership test `X→Y?` | O(log k) dependent random reads | O(1): one word |\n| count | O(1) using the `Size` field | O(N/64) popcount unless cached |\n| enumerate all members | O(k) pointer chases (cache/disk misses) | O(N/64) sequential words + `tzcnt` |\n| insert/delete | O(log k) plus rebalancing writes (several records dirtied, which also costs journal volume) | O(1): one word dirtied |\n\nIf one random miss costs about `M` sequential word scans (M ≈ 50–200 for DRAM, far more for disk), enumeration is faster with a bitstring once `k·M > N/64`, i.e. **ρ > 1/(64·M)**. That is roughly 1/3200 to 1/12800, which is *much lower* than the space break-even. Fewer dirtied records per update also means a smaller journal. These are estimates and LFS should benchmark them. Make `p`, `w`, the chunk size and both thresholds runtime-configurable, as the issue requests.\n## Implications for LFS\n\n1. **Architecture: one OS-agnostic core, thin adapters.**\n   - The `lfs-core` crate holds the on-disk format, allocator, journal, links store and indexes. Implications for LFS\n\nConcrete recommendations, ordered by confidence.\n\n1. **Adopt the united doublets file format byte-for-byte as the LFS \"links region\".**\n   - Header = 8 cells in slot 0 (§1.1). Record = 8 cells\n     `source, target, left_s, right_s, size_s, left_t, right_t, size_t` (§1.2).\n   - Link `i` lives at `region_base + 64*i` for u64.\n   - Keep `Reserved8` = 0 in the base format. LFS needs a version/feature word somewhere;\n     put it in a *separate* LFS superblock rather than in `Reserved8`, so unmodified\n     `doublets` 0.8 / C# `UnitedMemoryLinks` can still open the region. If space inside\n     the header is unavoidable, `Reserved8` is the only free cell, but whether other\n     implementations ignore a non-zero value there is **[UNVERIFIED]**.\n   - Use `u64` cells. A u32 variant (32 B records) matches what the C# `clink` creates,\n     but caps the store at ~2^31 links once external references are on.\n   - Enable external references (`half = 2^63 − 1`) so raw numbers (block numbers, byte\n     values, sizes, timestamps) can be stored inline as `-n` without consuming links.\n     This also matches link-cli's names store and the binary archive.\n2. **Use the SBT encoding, not C# AVL.** The `size` cells must hold plain subtree counts.\n   Implement the iterative (recursionless) SBT: no recursion in kernel/driver context,\n   and it is file-compatible with the recursive C# SBT. Ordering is `(source, target)`\n   for the sources tree and `(target, source)` for the targets tree (§1.7).\n3. **Keep the free list exactly as in §1.4:**\n   - threaded through `source`/`target` of freed slots;\n   - LIFO reuse (`attach_as_first` on delete, take `first_free` on create);\n   - high-water-mark shrinking on deleting the last link.\n   This is the existing \"fill the gaps with small links\" mechanism *for link slots*. The\n   issue's \"gaps between files filled with small doublet links\" for *data blocks* is\n   new; see recommendation 7.\n4. **Grow by a configurable step, and shrink on clean unmount like C#.**\n   - The reference step is 2^20 links (64 MiB). For an FS, make it a mount/mkfs option\n     (the \"configurable FS\" requirement).\n   - On a block device, \"grow\" means extending the links region into adjacent free\n     extents. Preallocating contiguous regions (ext4-style) avoids fragmenting the\n     region.\n   - Do **not** depend on `mem-rs::FileMapped` as is: it zero-fills on reopen with\n     doublets 0.8.0 (mem-rs#36). Use link-cli's `PersistentFileMapped` approach, or LFS's\n     own block I/O layer.\n5. **Make the journal the links DB itself, not a copy.**\n   - link-cli already writes transitions to `<name>.transitions.links`, a doublets store\n     of before/after link states (retention `infinite | sized:N | chunked:N:DIR`).\n   - For LFS, an optional journal can be a ring of link-state transitions stored *as\n     links in the same region* (or a sibling region using the same record format). That\n     satisfies \"embedded links DB so the journal is not duplicated\".\n   - Commit ordering (write the record, then the trees, then the header) needs design.\n     None of the inspected stores is crash-consistent: they rely on mmap plus\n     `sync_all`. **[design gap]**\n6. **Use Binary Links Notation v1 as the interchange, dump, debug and wire format,\n   not as the live layout.**\n   - It is compact, versioned, and has 96 golden vectors and 8 codecs.\n   - It preserves ids through gaps, and its store archive (§4.6) is exactly a \"links +\n     names\" snapshot.\n   - The issue's \"support binary links notation, maybe exactly\" is best read as: `lfs\n     export`/`import` and any network protocol speak Binary v1 *exactly*, while the\n     on-disk region uses the doublets record format. Binary v1 is a variable-width,\n     sequential encoding and cannot support in-place random updates.\n   - Reuse the `links-notation` crate (`links_notation::binary`) rather than re-implementing it.\n7. **Data and files: model content as sequences of raw numbers.**\n   - Prior art is `BytesToRawNumberSequenceConverter` with `BalancedVariantConverter`\n     (§2.2): content becomes a balanced doublet tree whose leaves are external raw\n     values. With 8-byte cells, pack 7 bytes per external leaf (63-bit payload) rather\n     than 1 byte per leaf. **[design proposal]**\n   - For large files, use extents: a link `(file extent_list)`, where each extent is\n     `(start_block length)` with raw-number leaves. File data stays in contiguous\n     blocks, ext4-like.\n   - The slack after each file's last block, and small files, can hold small doublet\n     links, which is the issue's gap-filling idea. That needs an allocator that hands out\n     sub-block 64-byte slots. **[new work]**\n8. **Bit-string indices are new work.**\n   - `BitString` (§2.1) provides the API shape: 64-bit words, min/max non-zero word\n     borders, And/Or/Xor, set-index enumeration and population count.\n   - A persisted variant could replace the free list and serve as an\n     \"is used / has usages\" bitmap per region.\n   - The issue's \"switch by usage % threshold\" maps naturally to dense bitmap vs sparse\n     SBT selection: for example, bitmap when more than X% of a range is set, tree\n     otherwise. No existing Links Platform code does this, so the format must reserve a\n     per-index \"kind\" tag. Put it in the LFS superblock, not in the doublets header.\n9. **Choose united over split for the mandatory embedded index, at least in v1.**\n   - Split gives better data locality: 16 B data records and per-link usage trees.\n   - But Rust and C# currently disagree on which references go to the external trees\n     (§1.3), and the Rust list mode is unfinished.\n   - Split can be offered later as the \"variable size indexing\" option.\n10. **Disk map (GitHub Pages).**\n    - RawDoubletsViewer shows the minimal reader: header struct, then `fread` records\n      until EOF.\n    - A static web page can do the same with `DataView.getBigUint64(off, true)` at\n      `64*i` offsets. Implications for LFS\n\nConcrete recommendations, ordered by confidence.\n\n1. **Adopt the united doublets file format byte-for-byte as the LFS \"links region\".**\n   - Header = 8 cells in slot 0 (§1.1). Record = 8 cells\n     `source, target, left_s, right_s, size_s, left_t, right_t, size_t` (§1.2).\n   - Link `i` lives at `region_base + 64*i` for u64.\n   - Keep `Reserved8` = 0 in the base format. LFS needs a version/feature word somewhere;\n     put it in a *separate* LFS superblock rather than in `Reserved8`, so unmodified\n     `doublets` 0.8 / C# `UnitedMemoryLinks` can still open the region. If space inside\n     the header is unavoidable, `Reserved8` is the only free cell, but whether other\n     implementations ignore a non-zero value there is **[UNVERIFIED]**.\n   - Use `u64` cells. A u32 variant (32 B records) matches what the C# `clink` creates,\n     but caps the store at ~2^31 links once external references are on.\n   - Enable external references (`half = 2^63 − 1`) so raw numbers (block numbers, byte\n     values, sizes, timestamps) can be stored inline as `-n` without consuming links.\n     This also matches link-cli's names store and the binary archive.\n2. **Use the SBT encoding, not C# AVL.** The `size` cells must hold plain subtree counts.\n   Implement the iterative (recursionless) SBT: no recursion in kernel/driver context,\n   and it is file-compatible with the recursive C# SBT. Ordering is `(source, target)`\n   for the sources tree and `(target, source)` for the targets tree (§1.7).\n3. **Keep the free list exactly as in §1.4:**\n   - threaded through `source`/`target` of freed slots;\n   - LIFO reuse (`attach_as_first` on delete, take `first_free` on create);\n   - high-water-mark shrinking on deleting the last link.\n   This is the existing \"fill the gaps with small links\" mechanism *for link slots*. The\n   issue's \"gaps between files filled with small doublet links\" for *data blocks* is\n   new; see recommendation 7.\n4. **Grow by a configurable step, and shrink on clean unmount like C#.**\n   - The reference step is 2^20 links (64 MiB). There is no allocation bitmap: free space is rebuilt at mount from the\n//! owners listed here (journal, chunk tables, chunks) and from the file\n//! extents in the inode records.\n== src/journal.rs\n//! The optional write-ahead journal shared by the file system and the links\n//! database.\n//!\n//! The journal is a fixed region (blocks `start..start + blocks`) holding at\n//! most one transaction at a time, always written from the region start:\n//!\n//! ```text\n//! descriptor block(s)  \"LFSJDESC\" seq count | target block numbers...\n//! data blocks          new contents of each target, in order\n//! commit block         \"LFSJCMIT\" seq count crc32(descriptors + data)\n//! ```\n//!\n//! On mount it is\n//! replayed if it is valid and its sequence number is the superblock's plus\n//! one (or the superblock is torn and the transaction carries block 0).\n//! Replaying is idempotent, so a crash during replay is harmless. Because the\n//! superblock (block 0) is always checkpointed last, a superblock carrying\n//! the new sequence number implies every other block is checkpointed too.\n== src/space.rs\n//! Block allocator.\n//!\n//! The allocation state is not stored on disk: it is rebuilt at mount from\n//! the owners of every block (superblock, journal, chunk tables, chunks and\n//! file extents). This removes a whole class of bitmap/metadata mismatches,\n//! and every block always has exactly one owner, which the disk map shows.\n//!\n//! Blocks freed since the last commit stay reserved until the commit lands\n//! (\"pending free\"), so a crash can never expose a reused block to the old\n//! committed metadata. Blocks allocated since the last commit are \"fresh\":\n//! writing them needs no journaling because no committed structure refers to\n//! them yet.\n== src/chunked.rs\n//! Relocatable arrays of fixed-size records.\n//!\n//! Links, inodes, usage handles and every size class of the variable-size\n//! store are [`ChunkedArray`]s: records live in small chunks (one block, or\n//! one record when records are larger than a block) that can sit anywhere on\n//! the device. Chunks are what fills the gaps between contiguous files, and\n//! they are \"liquid\": the allocator may move a chunk to let a file grow in\n//! place. A chunk table (one `u64` block number per chunk) stored in its own\n//! contiguous extent locates the chunks.\n//!\n//! New chunks get their blocks only at commit (delayed allocation), so the\n//! allocator sees the final set of new chunks at once and places each of\n//! them in the smallest gap.\n== src/varstore.rs\n//! Variable-size storage: power-of-two size classes from 16 bytes to 1 MiB.\n//!\n//! Every class is a [`ChunkedArray`] of fixed-size slots, so variable-size\n//! objects never fragment the device: they live in the same small,\n//! relocatable chunks as links. A slot starts with a `u32` length; length 0\n//! marks a free slot (free slots are found again at mount by that marker).\n//!\n//! Objects are addressed by a [`Handle`] that packs a kind tag, the class and\n//! the slot number into one `u64`, so a handle fits in a link-sized cell.\n== src/sbt.rs\n//! Size-balanced trees over externally stored nodes.\n//!\n//! The same algorithm (Chen Qifeng's SBT, as used by linksplatform's\n//! doublets) drives the trees embedded in link records and the per-link\n//! trees of the optional variable-size index. Node `0` is the null node;\n//! subtree sizes are plain counts, so a tree is byte-compatible with the\n//! doublets `size_as_source`/`size_as_target` cells.\n== src/links/mod.rs\n//! The embedded universal links database.\n//!\n//! A doublets store (every link is `index: source -> target`) shared by the\n//! file system and by users through the CLI and the `/.lfs` directory. The\n//! file system's own structures — inodes, names, directory entries — are\n//! ordinary links of this store, so one journal covers both.\n//!\n//! The optional variable-size usage index.\n//!\n//! For every link `X` and each role it keeps the set of links that use `X`\n//! as their source (or target). A set is stored in the variable-size store\n//! either as a size-balanced tree (24 bytes per user) or as a bit string\n//! (one bit per link in the store, bit `L` set iff link `L` uses `X`).\n//!\n//! Above the threshold a\n//! set becomes a bit string; it goes back to a tree only when the density\n//! drops below `threshold * hysteresis` so sets near the boundary do not\n//! flip back and forth.\n== src/links/records.rs\n//! Raw link records and their embedded size-balanced trees.\n//!\n//! * **United** — one 64-byte record per link, exactly the doublets\n//!   `UnitedMemoryLinks<u64>` record: `source, target, left_as_source,\n//!   right_as_source, size_as_source, left_as_target, right_as_target,\n//!   size_as_target`, with the links header in record 0. Two global trees\n//!   order all links by `(source, target)` and by `(target, source)`.\n//! * **Split** — 16-byte data records (`source, target`) plus 64-byte index\n//!   records shaped like the doublets `IndexPart`: `root_as_source,\n//!   left_as_source, right_as_source, size_as_source, root_as_target, ...`.\n//!   Every link roots its own trees of users (per-link trees keyed by the\n//!   other end); references to external values go to two global trees\n//!   rooted in the header, following the C# `SplitMemoryLinks` rule.\n//! * **Data-only** — 16-byte data records, no embedded index.\n== src/links/packet.rs\n//! Import and export of the links store.\n//!\n//! * **Store archive** — the whole store in [binary links notation] version 1,\n//!   exactly as link-cli writes it (`--export-binary`, spec §10): a links\n//!   packet without external references and with packed widths, where every\n//!   link keeps its address and unused addresses are section gaps, followed\n//!   by a names packet (external references, packed widths) holding\n//!   `address code-point…` per named link. The raw cells of external\n//!   references are 64-bit Hybrid values (`2^64 - v`), so they travel as\n//!   8-byte references and come back unchanged.\n//! * **Doublets file** — the `.links` file of the doublets library\n//!   (`UnitedMemoryLinks<u64>`): 64-byte records, the header in record 0.\n//!   It is byte for byte the record array of the united layout.\n//! * **`LiNo` text** — one `(index: source target)` link per line, with `$v`\n//!   for the external value `v`.\n//!\n//! [`Links::place_all`] imports at the original addresses (into a store\n//! where they are free); [`import_remapped`] gives the links new addresses\n//! and reuses links that already exist, which is how a mounted volume\n//! takes foreign links without touching its own.\n//!\n//! [binary links notation]: https://github.com/link-foundation/links-notation/blob/main/docs/protocol/binary-links-notation.md\n== src/fs/mod.rs\n//! The file system: files and directories stored as links.\n//!\n//! # Schema\n//!\n//! Links `1..=5` are the binary links notation marker points (`ONE`,\n//! `NUMBER`, `STRING`, `LIST`, `IDENTIFIED`); `6..=9` are the type points\n//! [`FILE`], [`DIR`], [`SYMLINK`] and [`CONFIG`]. Then:\n//!\n//! ```text\n//! inode     I = (TYPE, $slot)        slot of the 64-byte inode record\n//! name      N = (STRING, chain)      binary links notation string\n//! entry     E = (D, N)               name N in directory D\n//! binding   B = (E, I)               the entry points at inode I\n//! symlink   S = (I, N)               symbolic link I points at text N\n//! config    C = (CONFIG, N)          persisted runtime configuration\n//! ```\n//!\n//! Because a link is unique by its source and target, a name exists at most\n//! once per directory and every name text is stored once per volume. Hard\n//! links are several bindings of one inode; the parent of a directory is\n//! found from its only binding.\n//!\n//! # Data\n//!\n//! Every file is one contiguous extent. Growing tries, in order: growth in\n//! place (with `growth-percent` extra room), exact growth in place, moving\n//! the link chunks that block growth in place, relocating the file, and\n//! compacting the volume. Link, inode and index chunks fill the gaps between\n//! files, so the volume never fragments.\n== src/fs/file.rs\n//! File data: one contiguous extent per file.\n//!\n//! A file that must grow tries, in order:\n//!\n//! 1. growing in place with `growth-percent` extra room, then exactly;\n//! 2. moving the link chunks right after it elsewhere (they are small and\n//!    relocatable), then growing in place;\n//! 3. moving the whole file to a free extent that fits;\n//! 4. compacting the volume (if `auto-compact` is on) and trying again;\n//! 5. failing with `ENOSPC`.\n//!\n//! Extra room is trimmed when the last handle is closed, so a file never\n//! keeps more than one partial block of slack on disk.\n== src/fs/names.rs\n//! File names as links-notation strings.\n//!\n//! A name is the binary links notation string `(STRING chain)`, where the\n//! chain is a nil-terminated cons list `(c1 (c2 (... (cn 0))))` of external\n//! references. With [`NameEncoding::Chars`] every element is one Unicode\n//! code point, exactly as binary links notation stores strings; with\n//! [`NameEncoding::Packed`] every element packs up to seven UTF-8 bytes\n//! (`length << 56 | bytes`), so a 21-byte name takes 3 links instead of 21.\n//!\n//! Chains are built from the end, so names share suffix links and every\n//! name is stored once, however many directories use it.\n== src/fs/commit.rs\n//! Commit: one atomic transaction for the file system and the links\n//! database together.\n//!\n//! 1. New chunks get blocks (link chunks go into the smallest gaps when\n//!    `gap-fill` is on).\n//! 2. Blocks allocated since the last commit (\"fresh\") are written in place:\n//!    no committed structure refers to them, so a crash cannot expose them.\n//! 3. Overwrites of committed blocks and the new superblock go through the\n//!    journal, then are checkpointed in place, superblock last. If they do\n//!    not fit, the dirty chunks are first moved to fresh blocks\n//!    (copy-on-write), which leaves only the chunk tables and the superblock\n//!    to journal.\n//! 4. Without a journal every dirty chunk and table is moved to fresh blocks\n//!    instead, so only the superblock is overwritten in place.\n== src/fs/control.rs\n//! The virtual `.lfs` control directory in the root of every mounted volume.\n//!\n//! * `.lfs/config` — the runtime configuration as links notation; writing\n//!   `(key: value)` lines and closing the file applies them immediately,\n//!   without remounting.\n//! * `.lfs/map.json` — the disk space map read by the web visualizer.\n//! * `.lfs/links` — every link of the embedded database as links notation.\n//! * `.lfs/stats` — volume statistics.\n//!\n//! The entries are not stored on the device; their inode numbers sit at the\n//! top of the inode number space where no real inode can reach.\n== src/fs/map.rs\n//! The disk space map: who owns every block.\n//!\n//! Every block has exactly one owner (superblock, journal, a chunk table, a\n//! chunk of one of the arrays, or one file extent), is free, or is pending\n//! (freed since the last commit). The map is what the web visualizer draws.\n== src/fs/interchange.rs\n//! The embedded links database as seen by its users.\n//!\n//! Links are created, changed, deleted and queried next to the file\n//! system, and the whole store is imported and exported (binary links\n//! notation archives, doublets files, links notation text).\n//!\n//! User links share the store, the commits and the journal of the file\n//! system. While `protect-structure` is on, the links the file system is\n//! made of cannot be changed or deleted, user links cannot start at or\n//! point to them (so the file system never mistakes a user link for an\n//! entry or a binding), and a link other links refer to cannot be changed\n//! (links are shared by content, so changing one would change every user).\n//! The marker points `1..=5` stay usable as ends.\n== src/codec.rs\n//! Little-endian field helpers and CRC-32 used by every on-disk structure.\n//!\n//! All multi-byte integers are stored little-endian, so images are portable\n//! between machines (the doublets store uses native endianness, which is\n//! little-endian on every platform LFS targets).\n== src/device.rs\n//! Block devices: where an LFS image lives.\n//!\n//! The file system addresses the device in whole blocks. [`FileDevice`] works\n//! with regular image files and raw devices (`/dev/sdb1`, `\\\\.\\E:`) on every\n//! platform, [`MemDevice`] keeps the image in memory (tests, the web\n//! visualizer) and [`CrashDevice`] simulates power loss for journal tests.",

Links `1..=5` are the binary links notation marker points (`ONE`,\n//! `NUMBER`, `STRING`, `LIST`, `IDENTIFIED`); `6..=9` are the type points\n//! [`FILE`], [`DIR`], [`SYMLINK`] and [`CONFIG`]. Then:\n//!\n//! ```text\n//! inode     I = (TYPE, $slot)        slot of the 64-byte inode record\n//! name      N = (STRING, chain)      binary links notation string\n//! entry     E = (D, N)               name N in directory D\n//! binding   B = (E, I)               the entry points at inode I\n//! symlink   S = (I, N)               symbolic link I points at text N\n//! config    C = (CONFIG, N)          persisted runtime configuration\n//! ```\n//!\n//! Because a link is unique by its source and target, a name exists at most\n//! once per directory and every name text is stored once per volume. Hard\n//! links are several bindings of one inode; the parent of a directory is\n//! found from its only binding.\n//!\n//! # Data\n//!\n//! Every file is one contiguous extent. Growing tries, in order: growth in\n//! place (with `growth-percent` extra room), exact growth in place, moving\n//! the link chunks that block growth in place, relocating the file, and\n//! compacting the volume. Link, inode and index chunks fill the gaps between\n//! files, so the volume never fragments.\n== src/fs/file.rs\n//! File data: one contiguous extent per file.\n//!\n//! A file that must grow tries, in order:\n//!\n//! 1. growing in place with `growth-percent` extra room, then exactly;\n//! 2. moving the link chunks right after it elsewhere (they are small and\n//!    relocatable), then growing in place;\n//! 3. moving the whole file to a free extent that fits;\n//! 4. compacting the volume (if `auto-compact` is on) and trying again;\n//! 5. failing with `ENOSPC`.\n//!\n//! Extra room is trimmed when the last handle is closed, so a file never\n//! keeps more than one partial block of slack on disk.\n== src/fs/names.rs\n//! File names as links-notation strings.\n//!\n//! A name is the binary links notation string `(STRING chain)`, where the\n//! chain is a nil-terminated cons list `(c1 (c2 (... (cn 0))))` of external\n//! references. With [`NameEncoding::Chars`] every element is one Unicode\n//! code point, exactly as binary links notation stores strings; with\n//! [`NameEncoding::Packed`] every element packs up to seven UTF-8 bytes\n//! (`length << 56 | bytes`), so a 21-byte name takes 3 links instead of 21.\n//!\n//! Chains are built from the end, so names share suffix links and every\n//! name is stored once, however many directories use it.\n== src/fs/commit.rs\n//! Commit: one atomic transaction for the file system and the links\n//! database together.\n//!\n//! 1. New chunks get blocks (link chunks go into the smallest gaps when\n//!    `gap-fill` is on).\n//! 2. Blocks allocated since the last commit (\"fresh\") are written in place:\n//!    no committed structure refers to them, so a crash cannot expose them.\n//! 3. Overwrites of committed blocks and the new superblock go through the\n//!    journal, then are checkpointed in place, superblock last. If they do\n//!    not fit, the dirty chunks are first moved to fresh blocks\n//!    (copy-on-write), which leaves only the chunk tables and the superblock\n//!    to journal.\n//! 4. Without a journal every dirty chunk and table is moved to fresh blocks\n//!    instead, so only the superblock is overwritten in place.\n== src/fs/control.rs\n//! The virtual `.lfs` control directory in the root of every mounted volume.\n//!\n//! * `.lfs/config` — the runtime configuration as links notation; writing\n//!   `(key: value)` lines and closing the file applies them immediately,\n//!   without remounting.\n//! * `.lfs/map.json` — the disk space map read by the web visualizer.\n//! * `.lfs/links` — every link of the embedded database as links notation.\n//! * `.lfs/stats` — volume statistics.\n//!\n//! The entries are not stored on the device; their inode numbers sit at the\n//! top of the inode number space where no real inode can reach.\n== src/fs/map.rs\n//! The disk space map: who owns every block.\n//!\n//! Every block has exactly one owner (superblock, journal, a chunk table, a\n//! chunk of one of the arrays, or one file extent), is free, or is pending\n//! (freed since the last commit). The map is what the web visualizer draws.\n== src/fs/interchange.rs\n//! The embedded links database as seen by its users.\n//!\n//! Links are created, changed, deleted and queried next to the file\n//! system, and the whole store is imported and exported (binary links\n//! notation archives, doublets files, links notation text).\n//!\n//! User links share the store, the commits and the journal of the file\n//! system. While `protect-structure` is on, the links the file system is\n//! made of cannot be changed or deleted, user links cannot start at or\n//! point to them (so the file system never mistakes a user link for an\n//! entry or a binding), and a link other links refer to cannot be changed\n//! (links are shared by content, so changing one would change every user).\n//! The marker points `1..=5` stay usable as ends.\n== src/codec.rs\n//! Little-endian field helpers and CRC-32 used by every on-disk structure.\n//!\n//! All multi-byte integers are stored little-endian, so images are portable\n//! between machines (the doublets store uses native endianness, which is\n//! little-endian on every platform LFS targets).\n== src/device.rs\n//! Block devices: where an LFS image lives.\n//!\n//! The file system addresses the device in whole blocks. [`FileDevice`] works\n//! with regular image files and raw devices (`/dev/sdb1`, `\\\\.\\E:`) on every\n//! platform, [`MemDevice`] keeps the image in memory (tests, the web\n//! visualizer) and [`CrashDevice`] simulates power loss for journal tests.",

It runs on any `Read+Write+Seek` device (file image, raw device, in-memory, WASM).\n   - Adapters, in priority order:\n     - (a) **Linux/macOS: `fuser`** (MIT). Pure-rust mount on Linux needs no system libs to build. macOS needs macFUSE or FUSE-T at build time unless built with `macos-no-mount`.\n     - (b) **All three OSes: `nfsserve`** (BSD-3) localhost NFSv3. No kernel driver and pure Rust; the best path for macOS without a kext and for CI. Windows needs Pro or higher.\n     - (c) **Windows: WinFsp** for the best NTFS-like semantics. Because winfsp-rs is GPL-3.0, prefer **hand-written Unlicense FFI bindings to `winfsp-x64.dll`**, which WinFsp's FLOSS exception allows since the Unlicense is OSI-approved, or use **`dokan`** (MIT crate, LGPL DLL, no bindgen).\n     - (d) Later: **FSKit** Swift extension wrapping the Rust core (macOS 15.4+), and in-kernel drivers.\n   - RedoxFS (MIT, COW, fuser-based) is the closest existing template.\n2. **CI**:\n   - Core unit and property tests on ubuntu, macos and windows runners.\n   - FUSE mount tests on ubuntu (`modprobe fuse`, `apt install fuse3`; remove the non-setuid `/usr/local/bin/fusermount3`).\n   - WinFsp mount tests on windows (`choco install winfsp` plus a registry check; clang is preinstalled for bindgen if winfsp-sys is used).\n   - On macOS: build-only for FUSE, and NFS (`mount_nfs`) mount tests through `nfsserve`.\n3. **Anti-fragmentation techniques worth copying (simplified):**\n   - **extents** with a large or configurable max length (ext4 is capped at 128 MiB by a 15-bit length field; LFS can use 32- or 64-bit lengths);\n   - **delayed allocation** (allocate at flush, when the size is known);\n   - **per-file preallocation windows** plus **shared small-object arenas** (ext4 `mb_stream_req` = 16 blocks, `mb_group_prealloc` = 512);\n   - **free-space index by size class** (mballoc's largest-free-order and average-fragment-size lists, or a buddy allocator);\n   - **inline data** for tiny files;\n   - **flex_bg-like grouping** of metadata;\n   - **metadata checksums** (crc32c).\n   - ext4 still ages (FAST'17), so the strict \"no fragmentation\" goal needs either **online compaction/relocation** (like `EXT4_IOC_MOVE_EXT`) or the issue's idea: **fill gaps with small doublet links** so free space stays in a few large runs and small objects pack densely.\n4. **Single journal or commit for FS and database.** The JOJ literature (ATC'13, FAST'14 ×2, ATC'15) shows a 58–73 % to 5× penalty from stacked journals. LFS should:\n   - expose **transactions on links and file ranges** to applications, generalising F2FS atomic writes and SQLite's batch-atomic mode;\n   - make the journal **optional and per-file/per-subtree configurable**, as in the adaptive per-file journaling of Shen et al., with modes like ext4's `ordered`, `journal` and `writeback`, plus \"none\" for COW regions;\n   - keep checksummed commit blocks, as in JBD2.\n5. **Index selection rule:** for a link X with k users out of N slots, store its by-source and by-target sets as\n   - an **embedded tree** while `k/N < 1/(p·w)` (= 1/192 for 3×64-bit tree fields),\n   - a **bitstring** above that, with hysteresis (for example, switch back below 1/384).\n   - Better still, decide **per chunk** (Roaring-style: array ≤ C/m entries, bitmap above), so the rule does not drift as N grows.\n   - Make `p`, `w`, the chunk size and the thresholds runtime configuration in the superblock or a mount option. Precedents: Roaring's 4096 and btrfs's free-space-tree conversion.\n6. **Portability:** no advanced FS is native on all three OSes (only FAT32, exFAT and UDF are), so a Rust user-space LFS with adapters for all three fills a real gap. Ship a `mkfs.lfs`/`lfs-mount` CLI per OS and document driver prerequisites (macFUSE/FUSE-T, WinFsp/Dokan, NFS client).\n7. **Viewer:** compile the core to WASM for GitHub Pages. Render a Hilbert-curve block map (btrfs-heatmap), a linear defrag strip, per-file extent lists (filefrag), a free-extent histogram (e2freefrag) and a time-lapse of a workload.\n8. **Licensing:** keep LFS Unlicense. Allowed dependencies are MIT, Apache-2.0, BSD and Unlicense (fuser, nfsserve, dokan, roaring, bitvec, fatfs, ext4-view, redoxfs). Avoid GPL/AGPL crates (winfsp-rs, windows-projfs, ZeroFS, tvix) in the shipped binary, or isolate them behind an optional, clearly labelled feature.\n## 5. Implications for LFS\n\nConcrete recommendations, ordered by confidence.\n\n1. **Adopt the united doublets file format byte-for-byte as the LFS \"links region\".**\n   - Header = 8 cells in slot 0 (§1.1). Record = 8 cells\n     `source, target, left_s, right_s, size_s, left_t, right_t, size_t` (§1.2).\n   - Link `i` lives at `region_base + 64*i` for u64.\n   - Keep `Reserved8` = 0 in the base format. LFS needs a version/feature word somewhere;\n     put it in a *separate* LFS superblock rather than in `Reserved8`, so unmodified\n     `doublets` 0.8 / C# `UnitedMemoryLinks` can still open the region. If space inside\n     the header is unavoidable, `Reserved8` is the only free cell, but whether other\n     implementations ignore a non-zero value there is **[UNVERIFIED]**.\n   - Use `u64` cells. A u32 variant (32 B records) matches what the C# `clink` creates,\n     but caps the store at ~2^31 links once external references are on.\n   - Enable external references (`half = 2^63 − 1`) so raw numbers (block numbers, byte\n     values, sizes, timestamps) can be stored inline as `-n` without consuming links.\n     This also matches link-cli's names store and the binary archive.\n2. **Use the SBT encoding, not C# AVL.** The `size` cells must hold plain subtree counts.\n   Implement the iterative (recursionless) SBT: no recursion in kernel/driver context,\n   and it is file-compatible with the recursive C# SBT. Ordering is `(source, target)`\n   for the sources tree and `(target, source)` for the targets tree (§1.7).\n3. **Keep the free list exactly as in §1.4:**\n   - threaded through `source`/`target` of freed slots;\n   - LIFO reuse (`attach_as_first` on delete, take `first_free` on create);\n   - high-water-mark shrinking on deleting the last link.\n   This is the existing \"fill the gaps with small links\" mechanism *for link slots*. The\n   issue's \"gaps between files filled with small doublet links\" for *data blocks* is\n   new; see recommendation 7.\n4. **Grow by a configurable step, and shrink on clean unmount like C#.**\n   - The reference step is 2^20 links (64 MiB). For an FS, make it a mount/mkfs option\n     (the \"configurable FS\" requirement).\n   - On a block device, \"grow\" means extending the links region into adjacent free\n     extents. Preallocating contiguous regions (ext4-style) avoids fragmenting the\n     region.\n   - Do **not** depend on `mem-rs::FileMapped` as is: it zero-fills on reopen with\n     doublets 0.8.0 (mem-rs#36). Use link-cli's `PersistentFileMapped` approach, or LFS's\n     own block I/O layer.\n5. **Make the journal the links DB itself, not a copy.**\n   - link-cli already writes transitions to `<name>.transitions.links`, a doublets store\n     of before/after link states (retention `infinite | sized:N | chunked:N:DIR`).\n   - For LFS, an optional journal can be a ring of link-state transitions stored *as\n     links in the same region* (or a sibling region using the same record format). That\n     satisfies \"embedded links DB so the journal is not duplicated\".\n   - Commit ordering (write the record, then the trees, then the header) needs design.\n     None of the inspected stores is crash-consistent: they rely on mmap plus\n     `sync_all`. **[design gap]**\n6. **Use Binary Links Notation v1 as the interchange, dump, debug and wire format,\n   not as the live layout.**\n   - It is compact, versioned, and has 96 golden vectors and 8 codecs.\n   - It preserves ids through gaps, and its store archive (§4.6) is exactly a \"links +\n     names\" snapshot.\n   - The issue's \"support binary links notation, maybe exactly\" is best read as: `lfs\n     export`/`import` and any network protocol speak Binary v1 *exactly*, while the\n     on-disk region uses the doublets record format. Binary v1 is a variable-width,\n     sequential encoding and cannot support in-place random updates.\n   - Reuse the `links-notation` crate (`links_notation::binary`) rather than re-implementing it.\n7. **Data and files: model content as sequences of raw numbers.**\n   - Prior art is `BytesToRawNumberSequenceConverter` with `BalancedVariantConverter`\n     (§2.2): content becomes a balanced doublet tree whose leaves are external raw\n     values. With 8-byte cells, pack 7 bytes per external leaf (63-bit payload) rather\n     than 1 byte per leaf. **[design proposal]**\n   - For large files, use extents: a link `(file extent_list)`, where each extent is\n     `(start_block length)` with raw-number leaves. File data stays in contiguous\n     blocks, ext4-like.\n   - The slack after each file's last block, and small files, can hold small doublet\n     links, which is the issue's gap-filling idea. That needs an allocator that hands out\n     sub-block 64-byte slots. **[new work]**\n8. **Bit-string indices are new work.**\n   - `BitString` (§2.1) provides the API shape: 64-bit words, min/max non-zero word\n     borders, And/Or/Xor, set-index enumeration and population count.\n   - A persisted variant could replace the free list and serve as an\n     \"is used / has usages\" bitmap per region.\n   - The issue's \"switch by usage % threshold\" maps naturally to dense bitmap vs sparse\n     SBT selection: for example, bitmap when more than X% of a range is set, tree\n     otherwise. No existing Links Platform code does this, so the format must reserve a\n     per-index \"kind\" tag. Put it in the LFS superblock, not in the doublets header.\n9. **Choose united over split for the mandatory embedded index, at least in v1.**\n   - Split gives better data locality: 16 B data records and per-link usage trees.\n   - But Rust and C# currently disagree on which references go to the external trees\n     (§1.3), and the Rust list mode is unfinished.\n   - Split can be offered later as the \"variable size indexing\" option.\n10. **Disk map (GitHub Pages).**\n    - RawDoubletsViewer shows the minimal reader: header struct, then `fread` records\n      until EOF.\n    - A static web page can do the same with `DataView.getBigUint64(off, true)` at\n      `64*i` offsets. It can colour records as free (in the list), live, or tree root,\n      and overlay data extents from the LFS superblock.\n    - Ship test images in both doublets-raw form and Binary v1 archive form.\n11. **Licensing.** link-cli and links-notation are Unlicense (Public Domain compatible).\n    The licenses of the linksplatform crates `doublets`, `platform-*` and `trees` were\n    not checked. **[UNVERIFIED]**\n\n---\n\n## 6. Open questions / unverified items\n\n- The exact tree roots after a given insert sequence (§1.8). This needs a test vector\n  generated with `doublets` 0.8 (not run here, per the no-build constraint).\n- Whether C# and Rust both tolerate a non-zero `Reserved8`.\n- How much Rust split and C# split files diverge in practice when they hold external\n  references (§1.3).\n- doublets-rs `sequences`/`unicode` modules, C# `CompressingConverter`, and the frequency\n  indexes: not read.\n- Repos `lino-objects-codec`, `linksql`, `doublets-dev` and `Data.Doublets.Lino` were\n  cloned but not analysed beyond file listings.\n- Crash-consistency guarantees: none are documented in any inspected store.\n---\nbump: minor\n---\n\n### Added\n- LFS, the links file system: a block-device file system in Rust whose metadata is an embedded doublets links database (united or split indices, optional adaptive bitstring index, variable-size store with a threshold) and that shares one optional journal with it.\n- Files take one contiguous extent each; gaps between files are filled with link chunks, and online compaction keeps the free space in one extent.\n- Settings that can change at run time, stored in `/.lfs/config` and set with `lfs config`.\n- Links import and export: binary links notation, doublets files and LiNo.\n- The `lfs` command line tool: `mkfs`, `fsck`, `map`, `compact`, `put`, `get`, `ls`, `links`, `config` and `mount`.\n- Mount drivers: FUSE on Linux, FreeBSD and macOS (macFUSE), and Dokan 2 on Windows x64.\n- A disk-space map visualizer on GitHub Pages.\ndesktop-release.yml\nlinks.yml\nrelease.yml\nsecurity.yml\nworkflows.yml\n#!/usr/bin/env bash\n# Validate the repository's key documentation (issue #161).\n#\n# CI-CD-BEST-PRACTICES principle 12 asks for three checks on documentation:\n# size limits (scripts/check-file-size.rs), broken links (.github/workflows/\n# links.yml), and \"the documents that are supposed to exist carry the sections\n# other documents link to\". LFS should:\n   - expose **transactions on links and file ranges** to applications, generalising F2FS atomic writes and SQLite's batch-atomic mode;\n   - make the journal **optional and per-file/per-subtree configurable**, as in the adaptive per-file journaling of Shen et al., with modes like ext4's `ordered`, `journal` and `writeback`, plus \"none\" for COW regions;\n   - keep checksummed commit blocks, as in JBD2.\n5. **Index selection rule:** for a link X with k users out of N slots, store its by-source and by-target sets as\n   - an **embedded tree** while `k/N < 1/(p·w)` (= 1/192 for 3×64-bit tree fields),\n   - a **bitstring** above that, with hysteresis (for example, switch back below 1/384).\n   - Better still, decide **per chunk** (Roaring-style: array ≤ C/m entries, bitmap above), so the rule does not drift as N grows.\n   - Make `p`, `w`, the chunk size and the thresholds runtime configuration in the superblock or a mount option. Precedents: Roaring's 4096 and btrfs's free-space-tree conversion.\n6. **Portability:** no advanced FS is native on all three OSes (only FAT32, exFAT and UDF are), so a Rust user-space LFS with adapters for all three fills a real gap. Ship a `mkfs.lfs`/`lfs-mount` CLI per OS and document driver prerequisites (macFUSE/FUSE-T, WinFsp/Dokan, NFS client).\n7. **Viewer:** compile the core to WASM for GitHub Pages. Render a Hilbert-curve block map (btrfs-heatmap), a linear defrag strip, per-file extent lists (filefrag), a free-extent histogram (e2freefrag) and a time-lapse of a workload.\n8. **Licensing:** keep LFS Unlicense. Allowed dependencies are MIT, Apache-2.0, BSD and Unlicense (fuser, nfsserve, dokan, roaring, bitvec, fatfs, ext4-view, redoxfs). Avoid GPL/AGPL crates (winfsp-rs, windows-projfs, ZeroFS, tvix) in the shipped binary, or isolate them behind an optional, clearly labelled feature.\n## 5. Implications for LFS\n\nConcrete recommendations, ordered by confidence.\n\n1. **Adopt the united doublets file format byte-for-byte as the LFS \"links region\".**\n   - Header = 8 cells in slot 0 (§1.1). Record = 8 cells\n     `source, target, left_s, right_s, size_s, left_t, right_t, size_t` (§1.2).\n   - Link `i` lives at `region_base + 64*i` for u64.\n   - Keep `Reserved8` = 0 in the base format. LFS needs a version/feature word somewhere;\n     put it in a *separate* LFS superblock rather than in `Reserved8`, so unmodified\n     `doublets` 0.8 / C# `UnitedMemoryLinks` can still open the region. If space inside\n     the header is unavoidable, `Reserved8` is the only free cell, but whether other\n     implementations ignore a non-zero value there is **[UNVERIFIED]**.\n   - Use `u64` cells. A u32 variant (32 B records) matches what the C# `clink` creates,\n     but caps the store at ~2^31 links once external references are on.\n   - Enable external references (`half = 2^63 − 1`) so raw numbers (block numbers, byte\n     values, sizes, timestamps) can be stored inline as `-n` without consuming links.\n     This also matches link-cli's names store and the binary archive.\n2. **Use the SBT encoding, not C# AVL.** The `size` cells must hold plain subtree counts.\n   Implement the iterative (recursionless) SBT: no recursion in kernel/driver context,\n   and it is file-compatible with the recursive C# SBT. Ordering is `(source, target)`\n   for the sources tree and `(target, source)` for the targets tree (§1.7).\n3. **Keep the free list exactly as in §1.4:**\n   - threaded through `source`/`target` of freed slots;\n   - LIFO reuse (`attach_as_first` on delete, take `first_free` on create);\n   - high-water-mark shrinking on deleting the last link.\n   This is the existing \"fill the gaps with small links\" mechanism *for link slots*. The\n   issue's \"gaps between files filled with small doublet links\" for *data blocks* is\n   new; see recommendation 7.\n4. **Grow by a configurable step, and shrink on clean unmount like C#.**\n   - The reference step is 2^20 links (64 MiB). For an FS, make it a mount/mkfs option\n     (the \"configurable FS\" requirement).\n   - On a block device, \"grow\" means extending the links region into adjacent free\n     extents. Preallocating contiguous regions (ext4-style) avoids fragmenting the\n     region.\n   - Do **not** depend on `mem-rs::FileMapped` as is: it zero-fills on reopen with\n     doublets 0.8.0 (mem-rs#36). Use link-cli's `PersistentFileMapped` approach, or LFS's\n     own block I/O layer.\n5. **Make the journal the links DB itself, not a copy.**\n   - link-cli already writes transitions to `<name>.transitions.links`, a doublets store\n     of before/after link states (retention `infinite | sized:N | chunked:N:DIR`).\n   - For LFS, an optional journal can be a ring of link-state transitions stored *as\n     links in the same region* (or a sibling region using the same record format). That\n     satisfies \"embedded links DB so the journal is not duplicated\".\n   - Commit ordering (write the record, then the trees, then the header) needs design.\n     None of the inspected stores is crash-consistent: they rely on mmap plus\n     `sync_all`. **[design gap]**\n6. **Use Binary Links Notation v1 as the interchange, dump, debug and wire format,\n   not as the live layout.**\n   - It is compact, versioned, and has 96 golden vectors and 8 codecs.\n   - It preserves ids through gaps, and its store archive (§4.6) is exactly a \"links +\n     names\" snapshot.\n   - The issue's \"support binary links notation, maybe exactly\" is best read as: `lfs\n     export`/`import` and any network protocol speak Binary v1 *exactly*, while the\n     on-disk region uses the doublets record format. Binary v1 is a variable-width,\n     sequential encoding and cannot support in-place random updates.\n   - Reuse the `links-notation` crate (`links_notation::binary`) rather than re-implementing it.\n7. **Data and files: model content as sequences of raw numbers.**\n   - Prior art is `BytesToRawNumberSequenceConverter` with `BalancedVariantConverter`\n     (§2.2): content becomes a balanced doublet tree whose leaves are external raw\n     values. With 8-byte cells, pack 7 bytes per external leaf (63-bit payload) rather\n     than 1 byte per leaf. **[design proposal]**\n   - For large files, use extents: a link `(file extent_list)`, where each extent is\n     `(start_block length)` with raw-number leaves. File data stays in contiguous\n     blocks, ext4-like.\n   - The slack after each file's last block, and small files, can hold small doublet\n     links, which is the issue's gap-filling idea. That needs an allocator that hands out\n     sub-block 64-byte slots. **[new work]**\n8. **Bit-string indices are new work.**\n   - `BitString` (§2.1) provides the API shape: 64-bit words, min/max non-zero word\n     borders, And/Or/Xor, set-index enumeration and population count.\n   - A persisted variant could replace the free list and serve as an\n     \"is used / has usages\" bitmap per region.\n   - The issue's \"switch by usage % threshold\" maps naturally to dense bitmap vs sparse\n     SBT selection: for example, bitmap when more than X% of a range is set, tree\n     otherwise. No existing Links Platform code does this, so the format must reserve a\n     per-index \"kind\" tag. Put it in the LFS superblock, not in the doublets header.\n9. **Choose united over split for the mandatory embedded index, at least in v1.**\n   - Split gives better data locality: 16 B data records and per-link usage trees.\n   - But Rust and C# currently disagree on which references go to the external trees\n     (§1.3), and the Rust list mode is unfinished.\n   - Split can be offered later as the \"variable size indexing\" option.\n10. **Disk map (GitHub Pages).**\n    - RawDoubletsViewer shows the minimal reader: header struct, then `fread` records\n      until EOF.\n    - A static web page can do the same with `DataView.getBigUint64(off, true)` at\n      `64*i` offsets. It can colour records as free (in the list), live, or tree root,\n      and overlay data extents from the LFS superblock.\n    - Ship test images in both doublets-raw form and Binary v1 archive form.\n11. **Licensing.** link-cli and links-notation are Unlicense (Public Domain compatible).\n    The licenses of the linksplatform crates `doublets`, `platform-*` and `trees` were\n    not checked. **[UNVERIFIED]**\n\n---\n\n## 6. Open questions / unverified items\n\n- The exact tree roots after a given insert sequence (§1.8). This needs a test vector\n  generated with `doublets` 0.8 (not run here, per the no-build constraint).\n- Whether C# and Rust both tolerate a non-zero `Reserved8`.\n- How much Rust split and C# split files diverge in practice when they hold external\n  references (§1.3).\n- doublets-rs `sequences`/`unicode` modules, C# `CompressingConverter`, and the frequency\n  indexes: not read.\n- Repos `lino-objects-codec`, `linksql`, `doublets-dev` and `Data.Doublets.Lino` were\n  cloned but not analysed beyond file listings.\n- Crash-consistency guarantees: none are documented in any inspected store.\n---\nbump: minor\n---\n\n### Added\n- LFS, the links file system: a block-device file system in Rust whose metadata is an embedded doublets links database (united or split indices, optional adaptive bitstring index, variable-size store with a threshold) and that shares one optional journal with it.\n- Files take one contiguous extent each; gaps between files are filled with link chunks, and online compaction keeps the free space in one extent.\n- Settings that can change at run time, stored in `/.lfs/config` and set with `lfs config`.\n- Links import and export: binary links notation, doublets files and LiNo.\n- The `lfs` command line tool: `mkfs`, `fsck`, `map`, `compact`, `put`, `get`, `ls`, `links`, `config` and `mount`.\n- Mount drivers: FUSE on Linux, FreeBSD and macOS (macFUSE), and Dokan 2 on Windows x64.\n- A disk-space map visualizer on GitHub Pages.\ndesktop-release.yml\nlinks.yml\nrelease.yml\nsecurity.yml\nworkflows.yml\n#!/usr/bin/env bash\n# Validate the repository's key documentation (issue #161).\n#\n# CI-CD-BEST-PRACTICES principle 12 asks for three checks on documentation:\n# size limits (scripts/check-file-size.rs), broken links (.github/workflows/\n# links.yml), and \"the documents that are supposed to exist carry the sections\n# other documents link to\".
